1-1.q: How can I use the mind as a tool to escape negative thoughts or feelings?
1-1.a:
If you want to use the mind to rise above negativity, you first have to recognize that the mind itself is layered. There’s the lower mind, which reacts based on past experiences, and the higher mind, which has the ability to lift you out of those conditioned patterns. You have a choice: you can either let the mind keep running its old programs, or you can consciously direct it toward higher thoughts. That’s what positive thinking is—it’s using the mind to uplift itself. There’s nothing wrong with that. It’s a valid and powerful technique.

When you notice that your mind is starting to spiral into negativity, immediately engage it with something higher. Use affirmations, a mantra, or you can keep it simple and tell yourself, “I can handle this.” Just keep saying “I can handle this” over and over again. No matter what’s happening, no matter what thoughts are arising, just keep reinforcing that you can handle it. What you’re really doing is redirecting the mind’s energy. Instead of letting it drag you into the muck, you’re lifting it up to a place where you can stay centered.



At the highest level, the real work is not about battling the mind—it’s about learning to relax in the face of whatever it’s doing. You won’t always be successful, especially in the beginning. That’s okay. Start with the little things. When someone cuts you off in traffic, when the weather isn’t how you want it, when someone says something that rubs you the wrong way—practice relaxing. Just let go. Your mind will try to pull you into the reaction, but you don’t have to go there. If you stay relaxed, the energy that was about to get caught in negativity will actually rise up inside you. This is the transmutation of energy.

Over time, as you keep letting go instead of feeding the negativity, the negativity itself will start to dissolve. The mind will naturally quiet down because it will no longer be receiving reinforcement. The more you relax, the more the mind releases its grip. One day, you’ll look back and realize that the very things that used to disturb you no longer have the power to do so. That’s freedom. That’s the result of having done the real work.

1-2.q: How do I handle the narration in my mind that creates doubt, guilt, or fear?
1-2.a:
If you wish to work with your mind to rise above these lower thoughts, you have to see why that aspect of your mind has so much power over you. If you look closely, you’ll see that it’s because, deep down, you’re afraid you won’t be okay. You believe that if you make the wrong decision, or if things don’t go your way, it will somehow determine your well-being. That’s why the mind keeps talking—it’s trying to find a way to make you feel okay.

The important realization is that it’s your mind causing the problem in the first place. You’re asking a mind filled with doubt, fear, and insecurity to give you advice about how to be at peace. Do you see how absurd that is? The more you engage with it, the louder it gets. It can never give you the answer, because it is the problem.

Don’t try to silence the mind. Instead, step back and watch it. See its patterns. Notice how it pulls you in with fear and uncertainty, making everything seem urgent and important. When you truly see what’s happening, you stop taking the mind so seriously. You stop believing that its endless complaints and apparent solutions hold the key to your happiness.

You don’t have to fix the mind. You don’t have to resolve every thought or feeling. You just have to realize that you are not your mind. The moment you do that, you’re free. Decisions can unfold naturally, without struggle. Life can take care of itself. Your job is not to control everything. Your job is to learn to relax back into the seat of awareness and let go of the false belief that your well-being depends on getting what the mind wants.

1-3.q: How can I shift from personal to impersonal thinking?
1-3.a:
The impersonal mind refers to the deeper, more peaceful thought patterns that are not about your personal desires and fears. The bridge to the impersonal mind is to start training yourself to see the bigger picture. You must work with your thoughts to get off your addiction to thinking about yourself and on to thinking with a much larger frame of reference.

Every moment is an opportunity to shift your perspective. When you’re sitting in your car, before you start the engine, stop for a second. Notice that you’re on a little planet spinning in the middle of nowhere. That’s reality. Then start the car. When you arrive at your destination, before getting out, stop again. Recognize that you just moved across a small stretch of space on the surface of a vast planet, and now you’re about to step into another moment of your life. Do this every time you walk through a doorway, every time you pick up the phone, every time you engage with the world. It only takes a second, and it will train your mind to see beyond its narrow, selfcentered concerns.

If you don’t do this, what will your mind do? It will worry. It will desire. It will dwell on the past. That’s just how the mind operates if it’s left unchecked. But the mind can be trained. Just like you can train a dog to sit, you can train your mind to rise above the personal. At first, you might have to be firm: “Be still! Quiet down!” Eventually, it becomes natural. Instead of being lost in thought, you start to recognize the deeper reality of every moment. In that reality, there is peace.

1-4.q: Isn’t the mind helpful sometimes? Which part of my mind do I listen to?
1-4.a:
It is not a matter of choosing which voice of the mind to listen to; it is about sitting quietly deep inside and not being distracted by the noise the mind is creating. You have made great progress if you realize that your personal mind does not always give good advice. You must be comfortable not listening to all the personal chatter it’s creating. Once you can sit comfortably within, despite any noise the personal thoughts and emotions are creating, you will have achieved clarity. Now you can see what is going on at all levels of your being without being distracted by it. In this state of clarity, you will know which thoughts are helpful for interacting with the world unfolding before you.

You don’t have to listen to every thought. You are perfectly capable of seeing a thought for what it is: a temporary expression passing through your mind. You can certainly choose to listen to some of these expressions if they are of assistance to you. Especially your purely intellectual thoughts. The intellectual, analytical mind can be very good in that realm. But if you think that you are your thoughts, and you react to every thought you have—you’ll be in big trouble!

No one is suggesting that you ignore all your thoughts. Just start with the ones that have no value and rob you of your joy in life. You’ll be surprised to see how many of your thoughts fall into this category. For example, what is the advantage of being bothered by thoughts of the past? The past is over; it had its day. If it wasn’t pleasant, thank God it’s over. Why keep hanging out with thoughts that bring back the disturbance you felt when the event happened? That has no value, only cost. People get lost in such thoughts all the time, and these thoughts ruin their lives.

Since you are not your thoughts, you can learn to release these thoughts if they come up and focus on the beauty of life around you. Focus on more constructive thoughts that are raising you instead of tearing you down. This is true for all the personal, disturbing thoughts like: No one likes me, or I can’t believe I said that; I feel so uncomfortable. Wouldn’t it be nice if we weren’t haunted by thoughts of the past or bothered by constant self-judgement? What if we could always appreciate that we are alive and able to experience reality as it passes before us?

If you practice letting go of nonbeneficial thoughts, you will find that you in there, the one noticing the thoughts, have an intuitive wisdom that is deeper than your thoughts. We’re not talking about things like mathematics—your mind is very good at purely analytical topics. But with matters of life as they manifest before you, especially with interactions with other people, the thought-free, peaceful wisdom that comes when the mind is still is a much better guide. Your thoughts may not be able to figure it all out, but you will still know what to do. This deeper wisdom is found by centering in the awareness of being, not in the noisy thoughts of the personal mind.

1-5.q: How do I apply the teachings of letting go when I have an anxiety disorder? Is it really the same process as for those who don’t have psychological illness?
1-5.a:
It is important to understand that the Self—consciousness—is transcendent to all mental, emotional, and physical states. Since it is transcendent to the psyche, it is transcendent to the anxious psyche. Anxiety, no matter how deep, is just a state that the psyche is capable of getting into. It has nothing to do with the Self. The Self is the one that is in there noticing.

For example, how do you know you’re feeling anxiety? This is actually a deep question. You know because you are in there experiencing the anxiety. You are not anxious—you are watching an anxious psyche. The problem is, you tend to get drawn into it, just like everyone tends to get drawn into their psyche.

If you have been diagnosed with an anxiety disorder, the assistance of a professional therapist can be very helpful. Fortunately, in the end, the process of stepping back and observing the mind is exactly the same for you as it is for anyone wanting to grow spiritually. Your growth is to be able to sit in the witness and learn to be comfortable with everything you see. If you are having a good day, be comfortable having a good day. If you’re having a bad day, relax your shoulders, relax your belly, relax your heart, and say, “Oh, look, this is what it means to be experiencing anxiety.” The Self is watching the psyche, and what you’ll see is that you really can sit within the Self and simply watch, even if the psyche isn’t doing well. To the extent that you are able to sit in the Self, you will start to feel spiritual energy come in from behind. Even in the midst of an anxious psyche, you can feel uplifted; you can feel the joy of Self.

1-6.q: I have done destructive things in my life and caused trouble for others. I can’t seem to let go of the guilt and don’t know how to fix things for the people I hurt.
1-6.a:
We are sorry to hear you’re struggling with regrets about your past decisions and actions. Life is a place souls are sent to evolve, and that is exactly what you are doing—evolving. If you learned to play the piano, and you made mistakes at early recitals, but now you play wonderfully, should you feel guilty about your previous mistakes? Or should you look back and be grateful for the lessons you learned?

It is the same with life. You have the right to learn and work through your stuff. Regrets hold you back from evolving beyond your past. In the end, you should be grateful for your past since it helped you to wake up spiritually. You cannot undo the past, but you can take the lessons you learned and let them shine forth as beauty in the present. If someone were to ask you whether you would make the same mistakes again, you would tell them, “No, I would never do that again.” Well, then, you have learned. You are allowed to learn and grow through life.

Raise yourself and offer the most beautiful aspect of yourself to every person you meet. Do not hold yourself back with issues from the past. Bring light into the present. When these thoughts and emotions of regret come up, don’t suppress them; use affirmations to raise them. Repeat regularly: I am a being of great light. I have learned to bring love and peace into this world. Or, I am born anew every day. My past pain has awakened me, and I am ready to raise myself and others around me.

1-7.q: I find myself swinging between higher consciousness and getting pulled back into my mind. How do I handle this back-and-forth?
1-7.a:
When you keep getting pulled back into your personal mind from a higher state of consciousness, understand that this is completely natural. This is what growth looks like. If transformation were as simple as touching a higher state and staying there permanently, enlightenment would be effortless. That’s not how it works. You wake up to a greater awareness, and then you see—really see—what’s going on inside. You notice how your mind pulls you in, how your emotions rise and fall, and how old patterns grip you. That’s progress. The fact that you can see it happening means you are no longer lost in it.

The reason you continue to get pulled in is because throughout your life, you’ve stored unresolved experiences that you didn’t want to deal with. Instead of facing them, you pushed them away, and now they’ve built up inside you. Every time you get pulled back into your mind, it’s because something inside is being stirred up. A thought, a situation, even a simple word can trigger all that stored energy to resurface. When it does, you have a choice: You can resist it by willfully pushing it back down, or you can recognize that this is your moment of growth. You don’t need to fight it. You need to relax and let it pass through.

If you truly want to handle this back-and-forth, shift your perspective. Instead of seeing these fluctuations as a problem, see them as part of the process. When you find yourself back in your mind, don’t resist it, don’t judge it—just observe it. Breathe. Relax your body. Instead of getting caught up in resistance, let the energy flow. Each time you let go instead of reacting, you are cleansing yourself. You are breaking free.

You must understand that the goal is not some perfect high state where nothing ever pulls at you. The goal is to become so open, so clear inside, that no matter what arises, you remain centered. Growth is not about clinging to peace; it’s about letting go of whatever is blocking you from it. If you commit to continuously letting go, there will come a time when your lower self stops pulling you down. Instead, even your lower self will begin reaching up toward the light. When that happens, the struggle is over—not because nothing ever comes up again, but because you have learned to let it pass without resistance. Keep letting go and watch what happens.

1-8.q: How can I balance intellectual curiosity with spiritual growth?
1-8.a:
Your mind naturally wants to analyze, to figure things out, to seek knowledge, and that’s fine. But real growth happens when you stop trying to fit life into your mental constructs and instead surrender to the unfolding of life itself. If you truly want to grow, don’t just chase knowledge—seek truth. Truth is not found in the intellect alone; it’s found when you let go of the part of you that clings to preferences, opinions, and the need to control outcomes.

First seek the highest—seek God and liberation. In doing so, everything else will naturally fall into place. That means letting go of the part of you that constantly grasps for understanding everything. You don’t need to understand everything with your mind. The greatest understanding doesn’t come from thinking; it comes from the quiet mind that transcends thought. When you release yourself from the need to figure everything out, you will find yourself naturally aligned with something much greater than the mind.

The mistake people make is believing that they need to reconcile spirituality with intellectual pursuit, as if the two are separate. They’re not separate. The highest realization is not found by rejecting the intellect, but by going beyond it. If you use the mind to serve something higher—if your curiosity is rooted in a sincere yearning for truth, rather than personal identity—you will find harmony. But if you stay caught in ego-driven analysis, doubt, and attachment to ideas, you will only create obstacles for yourself.

2-1.q: How do I differentiate between suppressing emotions and allowing them to pass through naturally?
2-1.a:
When you feel an intense emotional sensation rising within you, and your body starts to tighten up, the key is not to fight it. Don’t get lost in trying to control it or force it to relax. The moment you start thinking, I need to get rid of this tension—maybe I’m not doing it right, you’ve already engaged with the mind’s resistance. That very effort to make it go away is what keeps it there. Instead of resisting tension, just relax the area around your heart. Don’t focus on the disturbance; focus on relaxing the heart.

Witness consciousness means you are simply aware of what is happening inside you without trying to change it. If tension arises, you don’t have to suppress it, fix it, or analyze it—you just remain aware it is there, breathe deeply, and relax the heart. Let the disturbing emotion come up. In doing so, you create space for it to pass. You’re not ignoring it, you’re not pushing it away, and you’re not getting pulled into it. You are just watching. The moment you stop resisting, it can naturally begin moving through you.

The reason emotions feel overwhelming is because the mind pulls your consciousness into them. It wants you to engage. If you stay centered and just relax and observe, the energy will eventually release on its own. You don’t have to do anything except allow it to come and go. You’ll notice that, without your interference, the tension you once thought you had to fix will dissolve by itself.

This is the difference between suppressing and allowing. Suppression is when you push the feeling away, try to control it, or judge it. Allowing means you let it be there without interference, trusting that it will pass. If you truly commit to this, you will find that your consciousness naturally begins to rise above the disturbance, and what once felt heavy will become light. The more you practice this, the freer you become.

2-2.q: How do I deal with low-level tension and anxiety?
2-2.a:
The fact that you’re noticing this disturbance is an important first step. The key is to not fight with it but simply relax through it. The moment you start struggling with it—trying to push it away or figure out how to get rid of it—you’re actually making it worse. It’s like a lake that has ripples. If you go in there and try to smooth them out with your hands, you only create more ripples. If you leave it alone, the water naturally settles on its own. Your mind and heart are the same way. When you resist what you’re feeling, you stir it up. When you relax, it begins to settle.

When you wake up in the morning and feel tension, don’t go into the mind and start analyzing it. Don’t ask, Why do I feel like this? or How can I make this go away? That’s just another layer of disturbance. Instead, simply notice it. Ah, there’s some anxiety. Just let it be there, and then relax behind it. You are not the anxiety; you are the one who is aware of it. If you can learn to sit behind it without reacting, you’ll see that it comes and goes all on its own.

The mistake people make is thinking they need to fix their inner experiences. You don’t. You need to learn to let them pass through. Anxiety, fear, uncertainty—these are just natural energy fluctuations caused by the ego. They don’t need your interference. Can you relax and allow them to be there without getting involved, watching them rise and fall like waves in the ocean? That is the practice.

Have you noticed that almost everything you worry about never even happens? Look at your life—how many of the things you’ve worried about actually became real problems? Very few. Yet you’ve spent all that time lost in worry, when instead, you could have simply let go and lived in peace. The next time tension comes up, see it, acknowledge it, and then choose to relax. Just let go, again and again. If you do this, in time, you’ll see that anxiety doesn’t have to control you. It can just be another passing experience, like clouds in the sky.

2-3.q: How do I handle overwhelming feelings of loss and sorrow when someone I love dies?
2-3.a:
When you feel flooded with feelings of loss and sorrow, the first thing you need to understand is that there is nothing wrong with those feelings. Your heart is capable of experiencing an entire spectrum of emotions: love, loss, joy, sorrow—all of it. The real question is not whether your heart will feel these things; it absolutely will. The question is whether you can handle it. Can you allow yourself to fully experience what your heart is expressing, without resisting it or getting lost in it?

Your heart is like an orchestra, playing all kinds of music. Sometimes it plays a beautiful, uplifting symphony, and sometimes it plays the deep sorrow of a funeral march. Why resist any of it? Why not appreciate the fullness of what it means to have a heart that can feel so deeply? You wouldn’t listen to a powerful, tragic piece of music and wish it didn’t exist; you would recognize its beauty. The same is true for your own emotions. The heart expresses, and your role is to honor that expression, not to suppress it or fight with it.

The problem comes when you identify with these emotions so strongly that they paralyze you. You say, “I feel so much love that it hurts.” Why should love ever be a problem? Love is beautiful. Even sorrow is beautiful—it means you have cared deeply about something. The key is to step back just a little, to create enough space between you and the emotions so that you can fully experience them, without being consumed by them. Instead of saying, “I can’t handle this,” relax through it. Let the energies of those emotions rise up to you, let them express, and then let them pass. If you resist, you get stuck. If you hold on, they leave scars. But if you simply allow them to flow through, they complete their cycle and move on.

This is exactly how you handle the death of a loved one. Rather than getting lost in overwhelming feelings, appreciate the depth of love that your heart is capable of. You don’t need to shut down or push away the sorrow. You need to be open enough to let it move through you. If you do this, your love will lift you, not weigh you down. Your heart will become a channel for the natural flow of life, rather than a place where emotions get trapped. In that openness, you will find a deeper connection—not just to your loved one, but to the very source of love itself.

2-4.q: Should I actively trigger suppressed emotions to release them?
2-4.a:
No, you don’t need to actively trigger suppressed emotions to release them. That’s not how this works. You don’t go down into the mess and try to dig it up—life will bring up exactly what needs to be released when it’s time. Your job is not to go searching for buried pain; your job is to build the strength and clarity to handle it when it naturally arises.

Think of it like fruit ripening on a tree. If you force it off too soon, it’s not ready, and it takes a lot of effort to ripen it artificially. You’re interfering with something that happens best on its own. The same is true for emotional purification. That pain, those suppressed emotions—they will surface when they are meant to, and when they do, you must be willing to let them pass through. That means staying centered, breathing, and not getting pulled down into them.

The mistake people make is thinking they need to do something with these emotions, like stir them up or force them out. In truth, you are simply watching something inside of you that is trying to release. If you start engaging with it, you’re only reinforcing its grip. Instead, relax. Let it come up when it needs to, and when it does, let it go.

You can even talk to the energy that is trying to release. You can say, “I see you. I know you’re there. I’m sorry I shoved you down all those years ago. You’re welcome to come up whenever you’re ready, and I will do my best to let you go.” That’s a completely different relationship than trying to rip it out of yourself. That’s love, compassion, and surrender. If you stay with that openness, in time, everything will release exactly as it needs to.

2-5.q: How do you know when you’ve worked through emotional pain?
2-5.a:
When you’ve truly worked through emotional pain, you don’t have to think about it anymore— it’s gone. You don’t sit there and analyze whether you’ve moved past it; you simply notice that it no longer arises in you the way it used to. There was a time when certain situations, thoughts, or memories would trigger something inside you, and now they don’t. It’s like driving home from work and realizing something happened today that once would have bothered you, but now you didn’t even think to be bothered. That’s how you know.

It’s not about making yourself forget or forcing yourself to be okay. It’s that the charged energy that used to cause disturbance has been neutralized. The white lines on the road are not calls to action—yet you see them. They are there, but they don’t demand your attention. That’s what happens when you’ve fully let something go. It becomes like any other passing experience. It once distracted your attention, but now it no longer controls your inner state.

Think about things from your past that you used to be obsessed with but have completely faded from your mind. When you were a child, maybe you had a toy that was everything to you. Then one day, you outgrew it. It didn’t take effort, and you didn’t have to make a decision to move on—you just did. That’s what happens when you truly process and release emotional pain. It’s not that you suppress it, and it’s not that you fight with it. It simply flows into the vast ocean of life and no longer pulls on you.

If the pain happens to come up again, that’s okay. Just take a moment to notice—Wow, this used to really bother me, now it barely affects me. That’s growth. That’s how you know you have worked through an emotional blockage.

2-6.q: I feel deep shame about some of the things I’ve gone through in my life. How do I free myself from these feelings and stop being consumed by them?
2-6.a:
In your mind and heart, there are stored impressions from the past, called samskaras. The shame you describe is due to a deep samskara trying to release, and that is causing the feeling of shame expressing itself in your mind and emotions.

How do you release a deep samskara? Love it; welcome it; worship it. It is what stands between you and God—so it is very holy. Don’t push it back down; welcome it up. And don’t be afraid of it, or you will never let it go; you will just keep protecting yourself from it. Understand that it is just suppressed negative energy from your past trying to finally get out. You don’t want it down there—help it release. If there is pain, relax through the pain and give it the room it needs to pass through.

Do not try to raise yourself by pushing your disturbed self away. Raise yourself by raising the shame up—offer it to God, to the Universe. Literally, hold it in your hands and offer it up. Don’t be ashamed that you feel shame. Rejoice that it is surfacing. Give it whatever time it needs and let it go with compassion. If you are willing to do this, you will open yourself to the cleansing process.

2-7.q: How can I handle overwhelming emotions and thoughts when they feel too strong to manage?
2-7.a:
When emotions and thoughts become overwhelming, you have to understand that the time to deal with them isn’t when they hit full force—it’s every single day leading up to that moment. You don’t wait until a powerful wave crashes over you to learn how to swim. You prepare in calmer waters, little by little, so that when the waves do come, you know how to stay afloat. Every moment of your life presents you with an opportunity to let go—small annoyances, frustrations, and irritations. If you practice releasing these little things, when something big comes along, you’ll already know what to do.

When you feel strong emotions rising up, don’t immediately get involved. Just notice. Watch them come. Watch how your mind starts talking. It wants to grab on to the emotions and spin stories about them. Stay centered for as long as you can. Breathe. Relax. If you get pulled in—fine. But come back as soon as you notice you fell. Don’t judge yourself, and don’t fight with yourself. The mind will try to convince you that you must do something about these emotions, that you have to control them, but you don’t. You just have to be able to let them pass through you.

Here’s the key—don’t identify with them. The emotions are not you. The thoughts are not you. They are just passing energies. The only reason they seem overwhelming is because you have made them personal. What happens when you stop doing that? They come, and they go. Just like everything else in life. Instead of getting lost in them, you stay behind them. You remain seated in your true Self, simply observing.

This is a process, and it takes time. But if you commit to it by working with the smaller things in your everyday life, you will find that even the strongest emotions can come, and they won’t take you down. One day, you’ll notice that there’s no longer a gap between noticing the tendency to fall and coming back—you remained conscious throughout. You have become established in the seat of Self, completely free.

2-8.q: I’ve been going through a lot of pain since my divorce. Should I continue allowing myself to feel this grief, or am I keeping myself stuck in suffering?
2-8.a:
The feeling of loss after a divorce is difficult for anybody, and it takes time to heal. This is how a spiritual person navigates the process: They go through the human pain, just like any other person, except they do not resist the experience. They constantly ask themselves, “Who notices the pain?” They are aware of the pain, but they are much more interested in where the awareness is coming from. If the heart hurts, they honor the heart’s right to feel these real feelings, and they just deeply relax and breathe through the heart. Just as if the heart had nostrils, you can breathe the pain upward, toward the point between your eyebrows (the spiritual eye). This creates a sense of openness and acceptance.

Ultimately, a spiritual person honors what their human aspect is going through, while at the same time using the experience to explore witness consciousness. Constantly be aware that you are not the pain; you are the one experiencing the pain. If it helps, from a centered position, reach down inside to get a big handful of the pain, and offer it up to God. Stretch your inner hands up way over your head and let the pain go out into the Universe. Behind it all is the peace of knowing that all things pass in time, if you let them. And because you went through them consciously, you become a greater being. This is how an evolved spiritual person goes through difficulty—and it is also how you evolve spiritually.

2-9.q: When heavy emotional pain arises, how can I increase my capacity to relax and release it?
2-9.a:
When you experience heavy emotional pain, it is important to understand what is actually happening inside you. Just like your body has an immune system that works to expel impurities, your psyche has an innate intelligence that is always trying to free itself from what has been suppressed. The pain you feel is not a sign that something is going wrong; it is a sign that something is trying to release. These deep-seated impressions, stored from past experiences, do not want to stay buried inside you. They are rising to the surface so they can leave. Instead of resisting them, you need to learn how to let them go.

Your job isn’t to fight with what comes up or try to figure it out. You don’t have to analyze it, label it, or even understand it. Your job is simply to relax and allow the process to unfold. It’s like giving birth—yes, it can be painful, but that pain is part of something beautiful. Just because it’s painful doesn’t mean it’s bad. Every time you feel resistance to what’s coming up, that is your moment to relax, to lean away from the disturbance, and to allow it to pass through you. The more you practice this with the little things, the more you will be prepared when the bigger ones arise.

The highest approach is to actually welcome what comes up, no matter how difficult. You don’t have to enjoy it or feel comfortable with it; you can just appreciate that it is leaving. Do you really want to hold on to the things inside you that disturb you the most? Do you want to keep them buried, where at any time they can unexpectedly take over your inner state? Wouldn’t you rather let them go forever?

The moment something painful arises, you can shift your perspective. Instead of recoiling from it, you can say, “Thank you. It is time for this to leave.” You don’t have to force yourself to handle it perfectly—even a small shift toward openness will help.

If you truly commit to this process, you will eventually experience something profound. As you continue to relax through the energy of old pain, you will reach a point where it begins to break free. What once felt like overwhelming suffering will transmute into something entirely different—pure, uplifting energy. People have described moments where they stayed open through deep pain, and suddenly that energy shot upward and became bliss. That is the natural flow of energy when it is no longer blocked by resistance. This is the journey of true inner freedom: welcoming what arises, relaxing through it, and allowing it to pass. Every moment of discomfort is an opportunity to become free.

3-1.q: What is the purpose of the ego?
3-1.a:
The ego is not some higher, divine creation with a grand purpose—it is a defense mechanism. It was born out of fear and identification, first with the body, then with the mind, and eventually with a self-concept that you built over time. At its core, the ego exists to protect something that doesn’t even need protecting: a made-up version of yourself that you’ve been holding on to. The real you doesn’t need defense, but the ego doesn’t know that. It reacts as if every word, every look, every moment of discomfort is an existential threat. It spends its life controlling, manipulating, and trying to ensure that nothing happens that might disturb it.

The reason the ego feels so real to you is because you’ve been feeding it your whole life. You spend more time defending your self-concept than you do defending your actual body. Think about it—if someone says something negative about you, you feel deeply hurt, even though no physical harm was done. If someone ignores you, you feel rejected, as if you’ve been attacked. The ego has convinced you that its survival is your survival, but that’s not true. You don’t need a made-up self-concept. The only reason you suffer so much is because you are identified with it.

What happens if you stop defending the ego? What if you stop protecting this false sense of self? At first, it will feel scary because you’ve never done it before. But the moment you begin to let go, you realize something amazing: You don’t need to build walls around yourself. Life is not against you. You are not this fragile being that needs constant defense. You are something much greater, something vast and free. The ego was just a veil, a mask you created out of fear. Letting it go is not losing yourself—it is finding yourself.

If you truly want to be free, you have to stop serving the ego. You don’t have to destroy it or fight it; you simply stop feeding it. You stop giving energy to its insecurities, its endless need for validation, its resistance to reality. When you do that, something incredible happens. You become open. You become light. You start experiencing life directly, without the constant interference of that voice inside. When that happens, you will look back and wonder why you ever thought you needed the ego in the first place.

3-2.q: What does it mean to let go, and how does that relate to the ego and identity?
3-2.a:
Your question is very beautiful because it means you’re starting to notice what’s actually going on inside. Letting go isn’t some mystical process—it’s the most natural thing in the world. Right now, you hold on to certain experiences and store them inside of you. When an experience happens, instead of letting it pass through, you cling to it. When you do that, you start to build a house out of all that stored baggage—brick by brick, thought by thought. That house is what you call your ego. It’s not some external entity controlling you; it’s just the accumulated stuff you’ve identified with. The moment you let go, the walls start to fall.

Why do you hold on to this house of stored thoughts? Because you think it’s you. You’ve built this whole self-concept based on what you like and don’t like. That’s why when life comes at you, you feel defensive. If something doesn’t match the identity you’ve created, it threatens you. That’s why certain things trigger you while others don’t—because they hit something you’ve



stored. But you’re not that stored stuff; you’re the one watching it. You’re the consciousness that sees it all passing through. When something hits your stuff and you feel a reaction coming up, that’s your moment. That’s the moment you get to choose: Do I reinforce the ego by resisting what’s coming up, or do I let go and free myself?

Letting go doesn’t mean suppressing or pushing things away. Nor does it mean pretending you don’t feel something. It means you stop resisting. The moment comes, the feeling arises, and instead of tightening around it, you relax. You let it disappear as if it were written on water. That’s what real freedom is—not controlling life so it doesn’t disturb you, but getting to a place where nothing has the power to disturb you.

Please don’t overthink this. Just watch. Notice when something inside gets triggered, and instead of getting lost in it, relax. Let it pass. You don’t need to analyze it, fix it, or make it mean something. You only need to let go. Every time you let go, you create space for something higher. Little by little, that space becomes your natural state. That’s what it means to be free. It’s not something you achieve—it’s what’s left when you stop clinging to what you are not.

3-3.q: Is letting go of the ego the ultimate goal of spiritual growth? How do I
3-3.a:
handle situations where the ego drives my reactions?

Yes, letting go of the ego is central to spiritual growth. The ego is a collection of thoughts and stored blockages that create a false self-concept. By observing the ego without reacting or suppressing it, you align with your true Self, which is pure awareness. Situations that provoke the ego are opportunities to release its influence. If you want to work on letting go of ego, practice not always defending yourself—let go inwardly and remain in the seat of witness consciousness.

Remember that when something feels personal, it’s often your ego feeling attacked. You should practice letting go of small irritations daily. Over time, this practice will help you handle larger challenges. Always take a moment to distinguish between constructive actions and ego-driven reactions. Even when someone’s actions warrant a response, formulate that response from clarity, not as a reaction to a hurt ego.

An evolved being does not try to eliminate or suppress the ego, as it is a natural construct of samskaras from the past. Instead, they work to release the blocked energy that sustains the ego. This process, known as transmutation, involves raising the energy coming up as ego and transforming it into a higher expression, such as love, compassion, and acceptance. By observing your energy patterns and addressing their root causes, you can redirect this energy constructively. This work liberates you from the limitations of ego-driven behavior and allows you to experience unconditional peace and fulfillment.

3-4.q: I struggle with insecurity and worry about how others perceive me. I realize that this worry is unnecessary, but I don’t know how to let go of it.
3-4.a:
Your question is very poignant and is a very human struggle we all share. The bottom line is that as long as you see yourself as separate from others and believe you are the self-concept you have created in your mind, you will continue to worry about what others think of you. You worry about this because your self-concept is something you made up, and it is easily challenged by the opinions of others. Let go of the whole model, and all worries of what others think of you will disappear. The deeper you let go of yourself, the more connected you will feel with everyone and everything else. The sense of “other” will start to fade away, and you will begin to experience that there is no difference between any other person and yourself. We are all the same, back behind the self-concepts we have made up.

In essence, you are not who you think you are. Be daring and decide to stop defending the self-concept you created—let go of yourself. Every time you feel this worry of other people’s opinions come up, relax and release, and remind yourself that you are not your mind, you are not your heart, and you are not your body. You are something very great—you are pure love and oneness. The love and presence of your true Being is unconditional and complete. It cannot be diminished by anything.

3-5.q: Am I worthy of love, and how do I recognize my worth?
3-5.a:
If you’re questioning whether you’re worthy of love, you need to take a step back and look at what’s really happening. You are sitting in the middle of an entire universe that created and sustains you. Your heart is beating, your lungs are breathing, the sun is shining—everything around you is supporting your very existence. Does that sound like a universe that decided you’re unworthy? No, it sounds like a universe that is overflowing with love, constantly giving to you without question. Where is this idea of unworthiness coming from? It’s coming from your psyche, from a small voice in your mind that is telling you a story that you’re believing.

Your mind has created a little box, and within that box, it whispers, Am I really worthy? Am I really loved? That voice is not reality. That voice is just old conditioning: thoughts and emotions left over from past experiences. You have to recognize that your mind is not qualified to determine your worth. The same mind that tells you one minute that you’re amazing will, the next minute, tell you you’re not enough. Why would you take that seriously? You are already infinitely worthy. Existence itself is taking care of you every moment, no matter what your mind says.

If you want to be free from this false sense of unworthiness, neither fight with the mind nor believe it. Just step back and gently talk to it like you would to a small child throwing a tantrum. Say, “It’s okay. I hear you. But I’m not going to let you run my life.” Take the hand of that scared part of you and lift it up.

The Bhagavad Gita says we should raise the self with Self and not trample down the self. You are the higher Self—the consciousness that is aware of all this chatter in the mind. Stop feeding yourself the false belief that you are unworthy and then looking outside for validation of your worth. Your worth is not something that needs to be earned or proven. It is something you allow yourself to experience by letting go of what is blocking it.

3-6.q: How do I differentiate between pursuing opportunities and acting out of ego?
3-6.a:
To differentiate between pursuing an opportunity and acting out of ego, you have to look deeper than just the surface of your desires. The ego is personal—it’s made up of your past experiences, your likes and dislikes, and everything you’ve built inside to protect yourself. If you feel a strong need to prove yourself, or if you feel like you have to get something to be okay, that’s ego. The personal self is always trying to manipulate life to match its preferences. But life doesn’t work that way. Life is simply unfolding in front of you, and your job is not to control it but to learn how to serve it.

When an opportunity presents itself, it’s not something you have to chase or create, or like or dislike; it’s simply there. If you’re caught up in your personal mind, you’ll constantly be trying to control which opportunities to take based on what you think you want. Have you ever noticed that what you thought you wanted often turns out to be wrong? The mind is not psychic; it doesn’t actually know what will bring you fulfillment. If you step back from your personal preferences and just serve what unfolds in front of you, life has a way of carrying you exactly where you need to be.

The reason this seems so difficult is because the personal self is still involved. In reality, the only question is whether you are serving your ego or serving life. If you’re asking, Should I do this or not? and the answer is tied to what you personally want or don’t want, that’s ego. If an opportunity comes, and you don’t feel a personal grasping for it but instead a natural opening to serve what’s in front of you, then it’s not ego—it’s simply life guiding you.

The highest way to live is to surrender to life’s unfolding. Instead of trying to make decisions based on your mind’s endless chatter, quiet down and let life show you the way. Stop thinking that you need to figure everything out. You don’t. Avoid using the intellect to satisfy personal desires or fears. Focus instead on serving the unfolding of life. Life built this entire universe without your help—it can certainly handle the details of your path. If you relax and let go of your resistance, life itself will take you exactly where you need to go, and you won’t have to wonder whether it’s ego or opportunity—you’ll just know.

3-7.q: How can I balance letting go with maintaining personal boundaries?
3-7.a:
You have to understand that what you call personal boundaries is actually just a structure built by your ego. Your mind has created a set of conditions that say, “I am okay as long as people don’t cross this line.” But who decided where that line is? You did. Or rather, your past experiences, fears, and conditioning did. You’re essentially saying, “If life stays within this narrow framework, I will remain comfortable.” But life doesn’t care about your framework. Life is vast, unpredictable, and uncontrollable. The real question is, do you want to spend your life defending your ego, or do you want to be free?

Letting go of your boundaries feels difficult because you’ve identified with them as if they are an extension of yourself. They aren’t—they are simply walls your mind has built to avoid discomfort. What happens when someone crosses them? You close. You tighten. You get upset. That is certainly not freedom. If you keep reinforcing these boundaries, you’re actually strengthening the very thing that causes you to suffer—your ego. Just look at your life. Look at how many times you’ve felt disturbed, offended, or hurt because someone crossed a boundary you set. Did that feel good? Did it bring you peace?

You have to start recognizing that the only reason you feel disturbed is because something inside of you is resisting reality. When someone says or does something that crosses your so-called boundaries, you have two choices: you can resist and suffer, or you can use the situation to learn to let go and remain open. Remember, the problem is never outside of you; it is always inside. It’s your own reaction, your own resistance, that’s causing the disturbance. If you can recognize that, you can begin to work with it. Instead of saying, “How do I maintain my boundaries while letting go?” start asking, “Why do I have these boundaries in the first place? Who set them, and what would happen if I let them dissolve?”

This doesn’t mean you let people walk all over you. Quite the opposite. True strength is being so open, so unshakable, that nothing disturbs your inner peace. If someone acts in a way that is hurtful or unkind, you can respond from clarity, not from defensiveness. You don’t need to create a wall of boundaries to protect yourself. You just stay centered in the seat of awareness and act from there. You do what needs to be done, but without all the inner drama. What you’ll find is that life becomes much lighter because you don’t get stuck in past disturbances. You’re just here, experiencing life as it unfolds, without resistance.

Don’t be afraid to let go of your boundaries. They are not keeping you safe—they are keeping you small. Do your best to let life in. Watch what happens when you stop protecting yourself from something that was never really threatening you in the first place.

3-8.q: I have been reading about “spiritual bypassing,” where people use spiritual practices to avoid dealing with deep emotions or trauma. Could your teachings on relaxing and releasing just be another form of spiritual bypassing? Am I truly healing, or am I just avoiding my pain?
3-8.a:
“Spiritual bypassing” is just another term for resisting or suppressing the samskaras when they come up. “I’m a child of God, pure and positive. I should not be feeling painful vibrations; therefore, I push them away so I can stay positive. I use mantra to get away from negative energy because I don’t want to be negative.” That is spiritual bypassing, and it is not really spiritual and not so healthy.

In drastic contrast, if you recognize disturbing vibrations from the past when they come up, and relax in the face of them, you are giving them the opportunity to release—not outwardly, but inwardly. Relaxing and releasing is not a way of avoiding pain; it is a way of letting the discomfort pass through you. The additional benefit of doing this is that you learn how to relax through difficult current situations instead of storing even more pain inside.

Welcome the purification you need to go through. This is the opposite of spiritual bypassing; it is spiritual cleansing. A truly spiritual being uses spiritual practices to remain centered as painful experiences pass through. They don’t use practices to avoid or push the pain away; they welcome the pain and remain completely open as it releases. That is the purpose of relaxing and releasing, and over time, it leads to the highest states.

3-9.q: Why do so many spiritual seekers get caught in the trap of spiritual bypassing?
3-9.a:
The spiritual path is about being willing to face the energies you have stored within yourself so that they can be released. It is never about avoidance. It is not about holding emotions and thoughts at bay and saying you are above them. Where people get confused is when they mistake suppression for transcendence. Suppression happens when you push the negative energy away and try to rise above it. Transcendence happens when you let the energy pass through without getting involved in it. You experience all the emotions and thoughts that come up as the stored blockage is released, but you don’t let them define you. You give them room to pass through inside, without resisting them.

Ultimately, spirituality is about letting go of the entire ego construct. Many people get lost because they develop a spiritual ego, which is just ego with a self-concept of being spiritual. The spiritual ego does the types of things that are called “spiritual bypassing” in today’s vernacular. The bottom line is, if you don’t like what’s coming up inside and you use will to push it away, that is avoiding spiritual growth. If on the other hand, you welcome the discomfort and use your will to relax and remain open while it passes, that is real spiritual growth. That growth leads to true liberation.

3-10.q: How do I reconcile spiritual ego with true spiritual progress?
3-10.a:
If you truly want to be more sincere in your spiritual growth, then understand this first: You are not here to be perfect. If you were perfect, you wouldn’t be here. Earth is a place where souls are sent to evolve, and the way you evolve is by facing the experiences that challenge you. You evolve by letting go of the parts of you that can still distract you from your seat of conscious awareness. It is not about making yourself into some ideal version of yourself. That creates spiritual ego. It is about relaxing and releasing the parts of you that still believe they need something from this world in order to be okay— including needing people to think you are spiritual.

Always remember: The struggles you face, the times you fall, and the moments you forget are not failures—they are exactly why you are here. Every single situation that tests you is an opportunity to let go. Just like a child learning to ride a bicycle—you will fall. But in that falling, you learn balance. You don’t fight the falls; you don’t make them wrong. You use them to grow. Likewise, when life challenges you, don’t resist the challenges. Allow them to refine you.

The key to sincerity is to truly do the best you can. That’s all that is ever being asked of you. The best you can is the holiest thing in your universe. If you put your whole heart into it, whatever comes back to you is exactly what you need to learn from. There is no shame in growth. There is no blame in not being perfect. There is only the process of letting go, step by step, as life shows you where you are still holding on.

If you make God, truth, and self-realization the polestar of your life, then everything you experience will lead you toward it. There’s no need to worry about where you are or how far you have to go. You just have to be willing. Be willing to release what is pulling you down. Be willing to surrender your personal self to something greater. Be willing to die to the small self so that something vast and infinite can take its place. That is sincerity. That is the path.

4-1.q: How do I cultivate focus and witness consciousness in my daily life?
4-1.a:
To cultivate more awareness in your daily life, you don’t simply force yourself to concentrate harder. That’s not how it works. You cultivate more awareness by letting go of what’s distracting your awareness. That’s the key. You’re already capable of being completely present and walking through life with total clarity. You could do that right now, but something is distracting you from it. Something inside keeps pulling your attention away.

Instead of fighting for more focus, work on letting go of what takes your focus away. Life is constantly giving you opportunities to see this. You get in your car, and suddenly, you’re worried about getting a flat tire because last week your friend had one. Why? There’s no greater probability of getting a flat now than any other time you’ve driven. But your mind has grabbed on to that past experience and is projecting it onto the current situation. That’s the moment to practice being present, remaining in witness consciousness. Don’t fight the thought; just calmly notice it and let it go.

Letting go is not just for the big things in your life. It is a powerful technique for building awareness in every moment. You can always find situations where you’re about to react—perhaps with worry, frustration, or inner tension—and instead, simply relax. Take that moment to let go of the pull the negative thought or feeling has on your awareness. Practice relaxing and releasing. That is how you cultivate awareness. It is not about controlling your mind; it’s about releasing the things that steal your focus in the first place.

Right now, this very second, you are capable of being fully present. The only problem is that you’re getting involved in your distractions rather than releasing them. Every moment of your life presents an opportunity to let go of something that is distracting your awareness from remaining fully present. If you commit to letting go, the expansion of your consciousness will take care of itself.

4-2.q: What is the concept of “falling behind things” in your teachings?
4-2.a:
When something negative happens in life, you immediately feel a reaction inside—fear, guilt, shame, embarrassment. The natural tendency is to resist the experience because it doesn’t feel good. You might suppress it, rationalize it, or even act out in response—but all of that is just avoiding what’s actually happening inside of you. The key is to become aware of what you are experiencing. Before you react or suppress, just notice what you are feeling. That moment of awareness is witness consciousness, and it is everything.

So, what should you do when you notice the reaction? Nothing. You don’t fight with it, and you don’t try to make it go away. That’s what the personal mind wants to do—it wants to control everything. The real work is at the level of consciousness. Instead of engaging with the feeling, relax. Let it be there. It’s not about fixing the energy you’re feeling; it’s about changing your relationship with it. You are not the energy—you’re the one who’s noticing it. If you stop resisting and allow the energy to rise up and pass through, you will begin to notice that you are behind the energy you are experiencing.

You are the experiencer, and it is the experience. Eventually, the distance between subject and object becomes great enough that you are no longer relaxing away from the experience, you are relaxing into the experiencer. That is the essence of falling behind.

The mind thinks it should be doing something with this energy, but all that does is reinforce the fact that you can’t handle it. If you fight with it, suppress it, or try to analyze it, you stay engaged with it. If you relax and let it move through, it will release. You don’t have to get rid of it—you just have to be willing to relax and handle the discomfort. Over time, you’ll start to notice that what used to disturb you doesn’t anymore. You don’t have to carry all this inside of you.

This is what it means to fall behind things. You are not lost in the disturbance; you are simply letting it pass through while you remain seated in awareness. That is how you let go. That is how you free yourself.

4-3.q: I don’t see how my personal life is “not personal.” I accept that events outside my influence are impersonal, but how does this apply to my immediate life, like my family, work, or my belongings?
4-3.a:
Thank you for asking your beautiful question about the statement that things are not personal. To begin with, from the point of view of the conscious witness, nothing is personal. It’s all just what you are experiencing. All clouds are the same—they are clouds. But if one reminds you of when you were flying a kite with your dad, that cloud becomes personal. Obviously, the cloud is no different than any other cloud, but you took it personally, so it seems personal. “Personal” is something your mind did to the cloud after it came into your psyche.

This is a difficult subject because we are not ready to look at things objectively. We are very invested in the personal mind. A first step is to understand, at least intellectually, that “personal” is something our mind does to a moment in creation that is simply unfolding in front of us. When you learn to transcend the personal, everything becomes miraculous, simply because it even exists. In this environment of total openness, true unconditional love and peace take over where personal used to be.

4-4.q: If you sit in witness consciousness all the time, do you stop experiencing human emotions such as love, fear, and worry?
4-4.a:
When you sit in a state of witness consciousness, you absolutely do experience emotions. Witnessing and experiencing are actually the same thing. When you sit in a state of awareness, you fully experience the world around you, as well as the thoughts in your mind and the emotions in your heart. You let it all come and go without clinging to it or resisting it.

The distinction between being in the seat of the witness versus lost in the personal mind lies in what you find yourself doing with what you are experiencing. In the seat of witness consciousness, you are no longer reacting to your inner experiences, judging them as good or bad, or storing them inside. You cease to create an alternate reality in your personal mind of what you want or don’t want to be happening. Ironically, you will find that in that state, every experience you have will touch you more deeply because you are no longer pushing your experiences away or clinging to keep them.

This state of awareness is not a dry, cold place where you don’t feel emotions. It is a vibrant, beautiful place where all emotions are permitted to come and go, leaving you clear and fulfilled. Over time, because you are not resisting and storing the lower emotions, the higher energy flows of love, inspiration, and awe will naturally replace the more reactive human emotions.

4-5.q: I have been working on watching my thoughts, and it is working to some extent. But the more I watch them, the more I feel caught in them. How do I break free from this cycle?
4-5.a:
Thank you for sharing your experiences with witness consciousness. The difference between watching the mind and true witness consciousness is enormous, but very subtle. It is the difference between “watching” and “seeing.”

Watching is a willful act that you are doing inside your intellectual mind. This is not the personal mind; it is the intellectual mind watching the personal mind do its thing. There is nothing wrong with this; in fact, it keeps the focus of consciousness from dropping into the personal mind. For example, imagine the personal mind is complaining about something.

Instead of getting involved in the process of complaining, you apply will in order to relax, step back, and simply watch the process, rather than being lost in it.

But true witness consciousness—simply seeing—is deeper than that. Can you glance at a wall in your house, with all its furniture and decorations, and instantly just see it? Don’t think about it or do anything about it—just instantly see it. That is a form of witness consciousness. You do not need your intellectual mind, your will, or any act of doership—it is simply the totally natural process of just seeing what is in front of you. When you can just see what is going on inside you with the same effortless ease, you are in the state of witness consciousness. There is no watching—there is just effortless seeing.

How do you get to the freedom of true witness consciousness? Instead of struggling to stay out of the mind, relax and release the pull the mind has on your seat of awareness. By relaxing very deeply, you are detaching your center of Self from the struggle of staying behind the mind. You are, in essence, saying you care so little about what the mind is doing that you can just relax behind it without interacting with it. If you truly let go during this deep relaxation back into the seat of Self, you will begin to feel freedom, peace, and spiritual energy. Don’t expect it; just let go of your struggle to control the mind. In essence, don’t try to win the tug-of-war—just let go of the rope.

4-6.q: My mind reminds me that I am supposed to be watching the mind. Isn’t that just mind too?
4-6.a:
As you become more centered in the seat of witness consciousness, you will find that there are subtle layers of the mind. The mind is not really the enemy, but we tend to be completely lost in the noisy personal mind, which causes quite a bit of suffering. As you have noticed, the mind can also help by reminding you to go deeper. It can and does voice wisdom, such as, Remember to go back to the seat of witness consciousness. However, this is still the mind, and you are still experiencing it. You might hear your mind say, Oh no, I’ve been following my thoughts again. It’s time to step back into my seat of consciousness. You, who are aware that this is the wise mind talking, are still separate from it.

The witness does not talk or even willfully listen. It is simply effortlessly aware of what it’s aware of. Those wise thoughts that feel deeper than the others are still thoughts. They are to be honored, but they are not you. In meditation, it is not necessary to stop the chatter of the mind. Meditation is about sitting behind the mind and letting it come and go—letting it be noisy, quiet, wise, or crazy—without being distracted by it. When you can sit behind every voice of the mind and simply observe it, nonreactively, as mind, then you are firmly seated in witness consciousness. From that seat, over time, you come to know the nature of your being, which is pure love, far beyond even the wisest thoughts of the mind.

4-7.q: What part of me is speaking when I’m in a conversation with someone? How do I know if my words are coming from a place of genuine presence, as opposed to conditioned responses?
4-7.a:
I can offer some pointers that will help you see what is going on. First, before you start speaking to someone, take a moment to see what is going on in your mind and your heart. You might see some anxiety coming up. If so, I would ask you to notice what thoughts are being created in the face of that anxiety. Don’t try to do anything about it; just notice your feelings and the resulting thoughts. Since you are a conscious, aware being, it does not take any effort to see your thoughts and emotions. They are right there in front of you—you can’t miss them. They are very powerful and prominent inside of you. The one who is noticing the thoughts and emotions is the essence of your being. Thoughts and emotions can change, but it is still you in there noticing they have changed. You are the witness who sees what is going on in there.

Once you have established yourself in this seat of objective awareness, you are ready to see what happens when you start speaking. Almost without exception, you are going to see that your inner thoughts and emotions are going to guide what comes out of your mouth. If your thoughts and emotions are defensive, your spoken words will be defensive. These thoughts and emotions are just the reactive sum of your learned experiences. If a friend told you something positive or negative about someone yesterday, your thoughts and emotions about that person today will tend to reflect that. If you actually speak based on these past personal impressions, your outer voice will be expressing the reactions of your inner thoughts and emotions.

So, what is your alternative to a purely personal discourse? If you work on yourself enough, you will be able to stay centered in the witness before, during, and after the conversation. You will be able to notice your thoughts and emotions as they arise and let these purely learned reactions pass through without influencing what you are saying. You don’t suppress or deny the existence of these inner thoughts or emotions; you just let them pass by, like you do with the wind.

If you take that moment to let go, then you can be standing face to face with the other person without all the inner noise governing what is going on. Now, you can speak from your deeper heart and your deeper intellectual understanding. Your words will no longer be personal reactions; they will be real expressions of the deeper part of your being. These communications will not be based on trying to get something; they will be based on real love, understanding, and compassion. You will be communicating in order to serve others, not to serve yourself.

4-8.q: What is the difference between using a mantra and practicing witness consciousness to release blockages?
4-8.a:
If you want to release a blockage, you have to understand the nature of what’s happening inside you. There are two primary approaches you can take: using a mantra or practicing witness consciousness. Both can be powerful, but they work in different ways.

A mantra is something you actively do with your mind. When you repeat a mantra over and over, you create a layer within the mind, almost like a song that gets stuck in your head. That mantra stays with you, and when disturbances arise, you have a choice—you can either place your consciousness on the disturbance or shift it back to the mantra. The very act of redirecting your focus to the mantra allows you to let go of the disturbance. It gives your mind something uplifting to hold on to, rather than being pulled into the chaos of thoughts and emotions.

Witness consciousness is different. It’s not about doing something with the mind. It’s about stepping back and realizing that you are not the mind; you are the awareness that observes the mind. The thoughts come and go, the emotions rise and fall, but you are the one watching them. You don’t have to fight with your mind, and you don’t even have to listen to it. Instead of engaging with what the mind is saying, whether it’s a mantra or a complaint, you simply remain as the witness. When you are fully established in this state, you don’t need to shift to anything; you are already free.

The key difference between practicing mantra and witness consciousness is that with mantra, you are giving your mind a positive place to rest— training it to hold on to something higher, rather than getting lost in disturbances. With witness consciousness, you go beyond the mind entirely. You sit in the seat of awareness, untouched by what the mind is doing. It’s like the difference between trying to manage the waves on the surface of the ocean versus sinking deep beneath them, where everything is still.

Both are valuable, and either can help you let go of blockages. What matters most is your intention. If your goal is to release and rise above the noise inside, then whatever practice you do with sincerity will serve you. Whether you use mantra to redirect your mind or witness consciousness to transcend it, you are taking steps toward freedom. The fact is, they both lead to the same place. If you do mantra properly, over time it will take you far beyond awareness of mind, just as witness consciousness does. Ultimately, what’s important is that you’re doing something to lift yourself beyond the disturbances, rather than trying to manipulate or control the outside world to feel okay. Let go, turn inward, and allow the process to unfold.

4-9.q: I carry a deep blockage that has significantly impacted my life. I am doing better but sometimes I lose it. If I try to sit in the witness, I actually feel more tension and discomfort. How do I release such a deep samskara?
4-9.a:
Thank you for your sincere question. The discomfort you are feeling when you witness your inner state is because you are still doing instead of just being. Witness consciousness is not the willful act of looking at or focusing on your thoughts or emotions—it is simply the act of seeing them. There is no tension or struggle involved.

Obviously, you know that you have thoughts and emotions. How? They are there, and you notice them. If they tend to distract you and pull you in, and you have to pull yourself out to see them objectively, that is an act of will and can create tension. You don’t have to first focus on a thought, hold it, and then try to let it go; you can just let it go without touching it. That is witness consciousness.

Practice relaxing when there is nothing pulling you in. Then notice when your awareness starts to get pulled toward a distraction. The instant you feel that pull, continue relaxing; don’t do anything except relax. Just release the tendency to get pulled in. Don’t struggle, just relax. That is real letting go. You don’t grab the distracting object and then let it go; you simply relax and let go as the primary act. Eventually, you will experience all of this as a very subtle energetic shift in your energy flow. Energy was flowing up; now it is being pulled in a different direction. Relax and let go; it will continue flowing up. Do this regularly and the subtle energy shifts through your mind and heart will become more pronounced. The more you practice letting go of the pull, the more witness consciousness will become your natural, effortless state.

In the meantime, you are doing fine. When you get pulled in, some blocked energy that has been suppressed gets to release by expressing itself. You feel better, temporarily. Just say thank you, pick yourself up, and deal with what comes next.

5-1.q: What does a blockage feel like, and how do I know when I have successfully let go? How do I know if I am truly releasing the energy or just suppressing it? Is there a specific sensation that indicates a successful release of a samskara?
5-1.a:
When things unfold in your life that hit your blockages, it is usually quite clear. For example, if the outer event is hitting something you have stored as negative, you may feel a disturbed emotional reaction such as fear, anger, or defensiveness. You may also experience tightening in your belly and chest. There is a sensation of tightness and resistance; you may even feel a sensation of heat. The mind gets very active trying to do something about the difficult energy that’s coming up. The mind comes up with ideas for what to say or



do to try to fix the situation, so that you don’t have to experience the disturbance. These are some of the inner reactions to your stuff getting hit.

More importantly, what does it feel like to release a samskara? The very second you notice that your stuff is being hit, you relax very deeply. Relax your shoulders, chest, belly, and any other areas of the body that have tightened. It’s important to know that this may not actually cause the emotions and sensations to subside, but it gives you room to simply be aware of them, rather than getting involved. You relax in the midst of the emotional reactions in the heart and the noise of the disturbed mind, even if your heart and mind continue reacting. And what you will notice is that as you relax, the reactions tend to not be quite as intense or strong.

The physical sensation that occurs when you relax and release may be different depending on how strong the blockage is. If there is a major experience of tightening, then the release might only feel like a slight softening around the edges of the tightness. It is very much like relaxing in the midst of stretching the body, as in a yoga asana. There is a point where the body starts to resist the stretch, and you feel the tightening. But as you relax and release around the edges of the resistance, there is a sense of opening, and the muscle will begin to give a little. The same is true for your blockages—you are relaxing on the edge of the energy that you’re holding inside yourself. The more you relax, the more space there is for that energy to release, because you aren’t holding on to it so tightly.

Some blockages can be very strong, and the process of relaxing and releasing needs to be applied every time the blockage gets hit. It could take a while, even years, for a blockage to fully release. But over time, it will continually get weaker and weaker. The more you can simply be okay with the blockage being hit, the less you will care about it one way or another. If you don’t care, then how long it takes to go away does not matter because you have already left it for a deeper place within yourself.

5-2.q: How can I stop storing new samskaras when daily life constantly triggers emotional reactions?
5-2.a:
When daily life triggers emotional reactions, the first thing to understand is that you never start by forcing yourself to be someone you’re not. The moment you think, I should be witnessing, I should be leaning back, I should be relaxed, you’re already making it about expectations—about an image of where you think you’re supposed to be. That’s not helpful. What’s helpful is honestly recognizing what you’re experiencing and simply relaxing in its presence. No judgement; just immediately relaxing. That’s already a huge step in your growth. That’s the doorway to witness consciousness.

Now, can you feel the tendency to get pulled in? That pull is real, and it’s very powerful. It’s not just an idea—it’s an actual force that pulls your consciousness down into it. Instead of fighting it or suppressing it, just notice it. Notice how it comes up and tries to take you with it. That’s enough for right now. Just seeing it, and recognizing its pull without immediately reacting to it, is the beginning of the real inner work. You don’t have to push it away, and you don’t have to go down into it. Just sit in the middle, breathe, and stay as centered as you can. If you fall, fine. Just get back up and try again.

This isn’t about suppressing emotions. People often misunderstand that. If an emotion is there, of course you feel it—that’s reality. The question is: Are you being pulled down into it, or is it coming up to you? That’s the difference. If you let it come up to you, it’s still being expressed, but you’re not losing yourself in it. You’re not feeding it more energy. You’re simply letting it arise and release without resistance. That’s a very high state, but you don’t get there by force—you get there by letting go. This requires the realization that for something to pull on you, you have to be holding on to it. The moment you stop holding on, it starts to release on its own.

Start with the simple stuff. When you feel the pull, don’t try to win some big battle—just see if you can stay present for a few minutes without getting lost in it. That’s it. If you can do two minutes, you can do three. And over time, something amazing happens; you stop getting caught, and those samskaras begin to lose their grip. But don’t force it—let it happen naturally. Just keep relaxing and releasing and you will be amazed by the inner changes.

5-3.q: How do I release pain from my heart? Breathing and releasing doesn’t seem to work for me. I am not sure how to let go of emotional pain.
5-3.a:
First, please understand that there is a real difference between wanting the pain to stop and wanting to actually release it. Most people think that if they practice witness consciousness, pain should instantly go away. That is not true. Just as physical pain is not itself the problem, but your body communicating that there is a problem, emotional pain is not itself the problem; it’s just your heart telling you that it has a problem. A wise person doesn’t want to just stop the pain; they want to get rid of the underlying problem altogether, so the pain is gone for good.

The first step in dealing with emotional pain is to change your relationship with your heart. Begin by thanking your heart for communicating that it’s having a problem with something. This is a means of accepting the pain and not trying to push it away. Once you have come into acceptance of the pain, you can focus on the cause of the pain. In just about every situation, you will find that the pain in your heart is due to a disturbing past situation that you suppressed, a samskara. You didn’t want to feel the discomfort pass through you, so you pushed it away with your power of will. This caused it to be stored in the heart, which blocked the energy flow through the heart. Inevitably, the samskara will attempt to resurface again and again, and it gets pushed back down each time because of the pain and difficulty it elicits.

To work with the samskara, you must learn to relax in the face of the heart’s release of pain. You can start by talking to the heart and welcoming the release, or by thinking about the advantage of finally getting all this junk out of you.
