What matters is that you are not pushing the pain back down. This act of acceptance will create the room needed to allow the cause of the pain to release. Eventually, you will welcome the pain because it is the doorway that leads to inner freedom.

The key is to accept the pain in the heart as a messenger that something is wrong. Treat your heart with compassion and caring, as you would a child in your care. Be willing to let the pain pass so that you can come face-toface with the problem itself. This is what’s meant by working with the heart directly. You do not need the thoughts of the mind in order to solve the problems of the heart. The heart wants to purify itself, but you won’t let it because you are afraid of the process. The greatest gift you can give yourself is to learn to become comfortable with the experience of the heart purifying. In time, the heart will thank you by singing beautiful songs of love and joy to you—all the time, unconditionally.

5-4.q: Can I let go without understanding what the blockage is?
5-4.a:
It is certainly possible to let go of a samskara without knowing specifically what it is or why you stored it. A samskara is simply blocked energy. When it comes up, you can relax and release without having to mentally process it. You are simply letting go of the disturbance without getting the mind involved with the “who,” “what,” “why,” and “when.”

Of course, it is certainly okay to know what the samskara is and why you stored it, but you don’t have to. You will find, as you let go of more and more of your blockages, the mind will become comfortable with the process and will no longer need to understand it all. In the end, you are not just letting go of the samskara around the specific past event—you are letting go of your inability to handle the disturbance caused by the cleansing process. Once you are comfortable relaxing through that level of discomfort, you will be able to handle discomfort of that level with all new and old situations.

5-5.q: How does letting go relate to discomfort and growth?
5-5.a:
When you sit with discomfort, what you’re really doing is facing the parts of yourself that you’ve spent your whole life pushing away. That vibration you feel—that subtle, uncomfortable energy—has always been there beneath the surface. You’re usually just too busy distracting yourself to notice it. The moment you stop and allow yourself to feel it, you begin to see how much effort you’ve been putting into resisting it.

The key is to stop pushing it away. When you let go, you’ll see that what was once unbearable can’t actually hurt you—it’s just energy passing through. The discomfort only feels overwhelming because you’re resisting it. If you stop resisting, it will rise up, get closer to your consciousness, and then pass through. That’s what real growth is. It’s not about getting rid of discomfort; it’s about learning to relax through it.

At first, it’s very scary not to protect yourself from the energy release. You’ll feel fear, but instead of running from it, you learn to let it be. There is nothing physically touching you that can hurt you. Learn to see it as just inner energy vibrating at an uncomfortable rate. Truth is, you feel shifts in your energy flow almost every moment of your life. You just don’t pay attention unless it’s strong enough to distract you from what you are doing. Every time you feel this discomfort—whether it’s frustration, fear, or pain—you have a choice: you can push it away and keep it buried, or you can say, “Come up. I want to see what’s really down there.” If you do that, something incredible will happen: the fear will lose its grip, and you’ll begin to feel lighter.

That’s how you grow. You don’t grow by avoiding discomfort—you grow by getting comfortable with it. The more you let go, the more life opens up for you. Instead of living in fear of what might come up, you become willing to face anything. You realize that no matter what happens, you’ll be okay, because you’re no longer controlled by the things you once pushed away. Now you are on the path to total freedom.

5-6.q: What personal approach do you take when releasing samskaras?
5-6.a:
There are many techniques for releasing samskaras. I am a naturopath in most things, so that is the path I follow with samskaras. My experience is that they will come up by themselves when they are ripe to be released. The question is: Are you willing to let them go when they come up? Since they were generally stored with pain, they will come back up with pain. You have to be willing to handle the disturbance they create without pushing them back down. If you keep your inner hands off them, in time they will release the energy they need to release and then fade away. When they are permitted to pass through, their energy is free to continue its journey through the universe.

The only reason the samskaras got stuck in you is because you resisted their passing through. Once you can let them go, they have no reason to stay inside you. Over time, you will realize that less samskaras means more flow of the energy known as shakti—more love, more passion for life, more inspiration, and a closer walk with Spirit. Eventually, you will learn to enjoy the disturbance samskaras create when they pass through, because it is “the pain that ends all pain.”

How does one withstand the pain of an activated samskara? Relax and release. Just like in a yoga asana, or during a deep massage, relax through the tendency to resist. The only difference is that with a samskara, the entire dance is inside. The moment you feel the energy get weird inside, let go, relax, and lean away from where you see the disturbed energy. Over time, this simple technique of relaxing and releasing will allow room for the samskaras to release on their own. And please don’t put any new ones in! Relax and release through the issues of today that previously would have gotten stuck in you. Do it right then and there, the moment the resistance starts. Don’t wait for even a moment—it will just get harder to let go as each moment passes.

Try to put aside fifteen minutes in the morning and fifteen minutes in the evening to clean out. Start the day clean; don’t bring stuck stuff from yesterday into today. Then finish the day with nothing new inside. If you want to call this meditation, that’s fine, but relentlessly let go of whatever comes up. And don’t limit this to your time on the meditation pillow or yoga mat; do it every moment of every day. That’s how you let go of samskaras—you let them go! If you do this, in time, a beautiful flow of upward energy will arise within you. It will feed you from inside every moment of your life. You will become whole and complete—self-effulgent. This is the awakened shakti. It will draw you into it and take you the rest of the way home.

5-7.q: How do I tell if worrisome thoughts in my mind are just samskaras resurfacing or are valid instinctual reactions to a situation?
5-7.a:
Instinct is very separate from the mind. When letting go of the personal mind, you do not have to worry that you won’t experience instinctual responses. If a semitruck is approaching and you are out walking in the middle of the road, you do not need your mind to tell you that you had better get out of the way. Instinct is very quick and direct—you will run first and think about it later. The basic survival instinct is quite independent of the personal mind.

Where people have trouble is when their past stored experiences, their samskaras, end up creating responses that are not instinctual, but driven by the samskara itself. Because the emotional response is so quick and strong, it can feel like instinct, but it really is the energy of the samskara getting hit. For example, let’s say you had a job when you were in your twenties, and the only time you were ever called in to speak with your boss privately, you got fired. You resisted the experience, and it got stored within you. Now, years later, you are doing great with your current job, and you are called in to talk with your boss. That meeting could be about anything, but the stored experience naturally gets hit, and you get this feeling of anxiety. Your mind tells you, I don’t know, something doesn’t feel quite right about this. Maybe I better not have this meeting. This is not an instinctual response that is warning you—it is your stuff getting hit.

Because most of our reactions are driven by samskaras, any time you are not sure if you’re listening to your personal mind or instinct, it is always better to first let go of your inner reaction. Let go of the fear and anxiety as much as you can, and don’t let it drive your actions. You don’t have to find your “real self” to know what to do. Just let go inside, and be willing to let life show you what is needed in every situation. Things will unfold, and if you are not acting out of reaction, what is being asked of you will become very clear.

5-8.q: How can I work with strong physical sensations, like a racing heart, that occur during intense triggers?
5-8.a:
When a strong physical sensation arises because a samskara is triggered, the first thing to understand is that it has the right to be there. Just like when you stub your toe and it naturally hurts, when energy that has been stuck inside of you gets activated, it naturally causes turbulence. That’s all that is happening. The energy is hitting a blockage, and the body is responding. The problem isn’t that it’s happening; the problem is that you don’t want it to happen.

Instead of resisting, try something different—welcome it. Just like you would comfort a scared child, you can hold space for this energy: “It’s okay. You’re safe. Come on up.” You don’t need to fight with it or make it go away. Let it express itself without pulling you down into it. The moment you resist, you give it more power. If you simply relax, breathe, and allow it to pass through, it won’t stay.

You don’t need to understand why it’s happening. You don’t need to analyze where it came from. Just let go of the part of you that wants to control it. It’s just energy moving. The less you interfere, the more it will release on its own. Over time, as you keep welcoming these experiences instead of resisting them, you’ll notice they lose their grip on you. They come, they pass, and you remain untouched.

That’s your practice. You don’t need to do anything but stay aware, breathe, and relax. Let the energy do what it needs to do, and you’ll see—it will pass right through you.

5-9.q: If I have a positive experience, how do I prevent it from getting stuck and keep moving forward? What is the best way to deal with positive samskaras?
5-9.a:
If you have a positive experience, the first thing to understand is that you don’t have to worry about it getting stuck. From the highest perspective, you want to let everything go so you can be fully present and clear in the moment. But you’re not there yet, and that’s okay. For now, it’s enough to focus on letting go of the negative samskaras—don’t complicate your growth by worrying about whether a positive experience is sticking.

If a positive experience uplifts you, raises your energy, and helps you let go of something, then great—enjoy it. There’s nothing wrong with appreciating a beautiful moment. Where you have to be careful is when you start craving to have it again. If you get attached to a positive experience, and start manipulating situations or people in order to recreate it, then you’ve turned it into something that can actually cause disappointment and suffering. That’s when a positive experience can hold you back instead of moving you forward.

Just say thank you. You had a beautiful experience in which something aligned with your preferences: wonderful. Appreciate it, acknowledge it, and then move on. If you cling to it, you block yourself from what’s next. If you can simply be grateful and keep going forward, life will continue to bring you more.

Ultimately, you will see that if you hold on too tightly to one positive experience, you close yourself off to the next one. For all you know, the next one might be even more profound. If you’re open, everything becomes a positive experience. The key is to stay in the flow of life—always letting go, always moving forward.

6-1.q: How do I deal with recurring preferences and their root causes?
6-1.a:
Preferences are the surface manifestation of deeper blockages and attachments. When a preference arises, whether for something or against it, acknowledge the preference with a sense of curiosity. Allow it to surface without suppressing or indulging it. This will allow you to look past the preference itself and be able to see its source. The source of your preferences is that your natural energy flow is blocked, causing you to need something outside yourself to compensate. In essence, preferences are the attempted solution for making you okay.

So, when preferences arise, accept them without trying to analyze or suppress them. Practice observing preferences without acting on them, and try to consciously relax in the face of the discomfort they may bring. Over time, as you practice welcoming preferences in this way, their deeper roots, which were implanted in the past, will naturally come up and dissolve. Each moment of release brings you closer to your authentic self, unburdened by external dependencies.

6-2.q: How do I handle anger and preferences when I’m unhappy with someone’s behavior?
6-2.a:
If you find yourself getting disturbed by someone’s behavior—whether it’s a coworker, a boss, or anyone else—you have to start by looking inside. Don’t start by blaming them. Start by asking yourself, Why can’t I handle this? The other person is being who they are, acting out of their own patterns and conditioning, just like you are. The real question is: Why is this bothering you? What inside of you is reacting negatively to their behavior? If you don’t ask that question, you’ll end up jumping from one situation to another—new jobs, new relationships—always hoping the outer world will change so you can finally be okay. But it won’t. Life is going to keep putting these things in front of you until you decide to work on what’s happening inside.

If you want to use the situation to grow spiritually, you can start practicing letting go of the part of you that gets disturbed. This isn’t about pretending to be okay—it’s about genuinely working with yourself so that you don’t get thrown off by every little thing. If you can’t handle the driver in front of you, how are you going to handle a difficult coworker? If you can’t handle your coworker, how are you going to handle your partner, your kids, or your family? Every situation that disturbs you is a chance to grow, to see what’s inside you that’s resisting reality. The truth is that life is not going to stop being life just because you want it to be different. The real work is inside.

Does that mean you should stay in a job or relationship that isn’t right for you? Not necessarily. But before you make any decisions, you need to own what’s happening inside of you. If you leave just because you can’t handle the situation, life is going to bring the same lesson back around in another form. Instead of running, start by working with yourself. Let go of the need for things to be a certain way for you to be okay. If you want true strength, practice facing the little things now.



Ultimately, the question is: Do you want to grow? If you always insist that life must conform to your preferences, you will spend your whole life struggling. If you’re willing to use every disturbance as a way to release what’s holding you back, you will find real freedom. The highest spiritual masters don’t avoid life—they embrace it fully because they are no longer resisting it. If you want to handle difficult situations, start by letting go of the part of you that can’t handle them. That’s the real work, and if you do it, you will see that all of life can be used for your awakening.

6-3.q: How do I let go of my preferences and opinions without denying my individuality?
6-3.a:
You don’t have to deny your preferences or opinions, but you do have to learn how to relate to them correctly. There are many different aspects of your being. There’s your body, emotions, and thoughts—and then there is you, the consciousness that is aware of all of these. The mistake is thinking that your preferences define you. They do not. They are simply conditioned responses based on past experiences, just like Pavlov’s dogs salivating at a bell. You had an experience, it got stored inside, and now that past impression is shaping how you react. The question is not whether you have preferences—the question is, what do you do with them?

If a preference arises, neither suppress it nor blindly follow it. Simply notice it. If someone offers you two foods, one that always upsets your stomach and another that you love, of course you’ll have a preference. That’s fine. But if you’re starving and someone offers you food you’re unfamiliar with, do you let your preference stop you from eating? That’s the difference. You don’t let preference control you; you use wisdom to make decisions in spite of your preferences, not because of them.

If a strong preference or opinion arises, sit back and observe. Watch the part of you that insists, “I want this” or “I don’t want that.” See it for what it is—just a pattern playing out. If you cling to it, it owns you. If you fight it, it owns you. Instead, let it pass through, and allow life to unfold beyond the limits of your personal conditioning. When you stop letting preference dictate your actions, you don’t lose yourself—you free yourself.

6-4.q: Aren’t there some preferences that are universal? For example, who wants to get a terminal illness? If something like that happens, how do we deal with it spiritually?
6-4.a:
If you have a terminal illness, it has nothing to do with preference. It’s not always easy to accept, but you need to come to terms with the fact that the body is ill and is going to pass fairly soon. Either you do not accept that fact, which will cause more psychological suffering on top of the physical issues, or you do your best to let go of the inner resistance and work to find peace in your final days. That is using the situation for your spiritual growth.

On the other hand, if you do not have a terminal illness, but your mind is causing suffering because of the possibility that you might get one, this is where your preference is causing unnecessary suffering. In this situation, look inside and see why you would do such a destructive thing. Nothing is wrong, but since you don’t want it to be wrong later, you suffer now. In other words, life is not doing this to you; you are doing this to yourself. You need to look deeper and see why your mind would do such a thing.

What you will see is that you are blocked due to past experiences that you have held inside. These blockages are preventing your natural energy flow and leaving you weak and worried about your future. If you remove these underlying blockages, you will be filled with energy and strength, and experience great love and inspiration. When that is your inner state, there are no desires or fears—you are too filled with deep contentment, no matter what is happening. You know that you can handle whatever happens, so why worry about it?

Learn to embrace life and participate in her events with acceptance, passion, and the love of getting to experience your years on the planet. Please don’t ruin your life because it doesn’t match your preference system.

6-5.q: You teach about how our personal preferences can distort reality. What about our personal values? Do values serve a purpose in one’s spiritual journey, or are they also just preferences?
6-5.a:
Your question shows that you have a very good objective understanding of the concepts formed in your mind and heart. We are programmed by our environment. If you grew up in a culture that lived off hunting, you would not think anything about eating meat. If you grew up in one of Gandhi’s ashrams, you would find the killing and eating of animals immoral. Furthermore, you would not hold these values just for yourself; you would use them to judge others as well.

Since we all have had different life experiences, it is natural that we have different values. But surely there are some universal values that are right for everyone. For example, the First Commandment says: Thou shalt not kill. Still, we humans have found many exceptions to that divine commandment. We kill in “righteous” wars (for instance, working to stop Hitler), we execute prisoners, and so on. No matter what your values are, surely not everyone agrees with them.

So how do you live a life without values? You don’t. You have values, just as you have a body, a mind, and a heart. Spirituality is not about living a life without these, nor is it about living life without values. It is natural that you have formed values over the course of your life, and they can change based on new experiences. Accept that this is going to naturally happen, but also accept that others have formed different values they feel just as strongly about as you do yours. That is the key to growing beyond your personal self. You have a personal self, but you can objectively transcend the concept that your view of things is right. It is just your personal view, and others see things differently. Strive to be the one that understands why there are these differences, accepts their reality, and works to bring harmony.

By all means, live and work for your values, but be open to others. Do not let your values cause your heart to close to the rest of the world.

6-6.q: What is your take on striving to satisfy your preferences?
6-6.a:
There is a natural harmony in all of life. Every aspect of life serves the whole. Plants grow out of soil, water, and sunlight, and animals eat the plants, and when they die, their bodies go back to the soil. Everything is serving the cycle of creation. When we are in harmony with the whole, serving the moments presented before us, we are doing our part in life. It is called doing our dharma, and it is also referred to as being in the Tao. Participating in this harmony calls on us to use our bodies, our minds, and the inspiration and creativity from our hearts. When we live that way, we are in harmony with life, and we evolve through the experiences we have.

When we get personally blocked because we are unwilling to accept the flow of life as it passes before us, we bring disturbance into our world. To be able to handle this inner disturbance, we use our minds to try to figure out what needs to happen that will make us feel better and not worse. That is what we call our preferences. They are very personal, and they couldn’t care less about serving life as it is. They only care about ourselves and the way we want life to be. That is the cause of all wars, inequality, hatred, and prejudice. We all want life to be our way, and we struggle to make it be that way.

As we grow spiritually, we learn to let go of these self-centered thoughts and emotions. As they thin out, so do our personal preferences. More and more, we see what life is asking of us, and we are willing to serve it. We are coming into harmony with the whole. Eventually, that is our only inspiration: to serve creation as it unfolds before us. As our blockages fall off because we are not feeding them, a spontaneous joy wells up inside. This joy is unconditional. It doesn’t need things to be a certain way in order to feel love and passion for all of life. Surrender of the personal, and service of the whole, becomes our way of life. In the end, we have attracted to ourselves the highest possible state of being by surrendering our will to the force that is creating everything.

6-7.q: How can I manage my desire for wealth and the anxiety it brings?
6-7.a:
If your mind is constantly striving for wealth and success, and it brings you anxiety and fear, the answer isn’t to try to push those thoughts away or suppress them. You need to understand why they are there in the first place. Instead of resisting, ask yourself: Why do I want wealth so badly? What do I believe it will give me? The mind doesn’t just want things randomly; it wants things because it believes they will solve something. It believes that if you achieve wealth, for instance, you will finally be okay. That’s the misunderstanding—you’re looking for external wealth to fix internal problems.

There is nothing wrong with wealth itself. Wealth is not the problem. The issue is why you feel you need it. If you think that being rich will give you status, respect, security, or the freedom to do what you want, then the real question is: Why do you feel like you’re not okay without these things? The drive for wealth is just a symptom of a deeper insecurity. If you were already whole and at peace, wealth would simply be wealth—something neutral, neither good nor bad. But if you believe it will complete you, then you are setting yourself up for a never-ending chase, because no amount of money will ever be enough to make you feel whole.

Think about it: What happens when people actually become rich? They win the lottery, for example, and suddenly, everyone wants a piece of them. They get tangled in financial concerns, lawsuits, and people treating them like a bank instead of a person. Wealth itself doesn’t bring peace—it often brings more things to worry about. What you really want is what you think wealth will give you. You want to feel safe and free from worry. Those feelings don’t come from money—they come from achieving unconditional inner peace.

Instead of trying to force yourself to stop desiring wealth, go deeper. Look at the part of you that believes you need it to be okay. Be kind to that part of yourself. Don’t reject it or fight it—just observe it with compassion and curiosity. Why is it there? What is it really afraid of? If you work at this level, you will no longer be controlled by the endless pursuit of external things. Instead, you will realize that what you were looking for was never out there in the first place. The peace, security, and wholeness you seek are already inside of you.

6-8.q: How do I handle my preferences without projecting expectations onto moments?
6-8.a:
Preferences are natural. You don’t need to deny them or suppress them— they’re just there. The real question is: Why do you prefer one thing over another? If you look closely, there’s always a reason. Something inside you has determined that one outcome is better than another, and that’s fine. But when your preferences start turning into rigid expectations—when you tell life, “I can only be okay if things go my way”—that’s when you suffer. The problem is not having preferences; the problem is believing that life must conform to them.

Look at how life actually works. Does it always give you what you want? Of course not. Reality unfolds however it unfolds, and sometimes that aligns with your preferences, and sometimes it doesn’t. If you’re only happy when things match what you want, you’re setting yourself up for a lifetime of struggle. The world is not going to mold itself around your desires. The key is to recognize your preferences but not demand that they be fulfilled. If you do that, you will find that you are open to a much wider range of experiences, and life becomes a lot easier.

One thing you can do with your preferences is instead of getting rid of them, expand them. What if you learned to prefer everything? If you train yourself to embrace whatever happens, then suddenly, you’re free. If the driver in front of you is slow, instead of resisting and getting frustrated, just prefer the opportunity to slow down for a moment. If you get criticized at work, instead of getting upset, be excited for the opportunity to improve yourself. When you approach life in this way, you are not getting rid of preferences— you are expanding them to include the miracle of life as it is.

Ultimately, reality always wins. It doesn’t care about your preferences. The sooner you align yourself with what is, instead of what you think should be, the more peace you will feel inside. So, please, don’t fight with your preferences, and don’t fight with life. Let them both be, and just watch. You’ll start to see that you don’t have to control everything to be okay. You’re already okay—life is just unfolding, and you’re simply here to experience it.

7-1.q: How can I not feel resistance during tragic events?
7-1.a:
When you are faced with a tragic event, the first thing you must understand is that resistance will only make it worse. If you fight against reality, if you resist what’s happening, all you are doing is adding unnecessary suffering on top of an already difficult situation. But if you accept what is unfolding—not out of weakness, but out of a deep understanding that this is the nature of life—you will find you can move through even the hardest experiences with grace. You are here to grow, and every experience, no matter how painful, is part of that growth.

Truth is, you don’t know how you’ll handle extreme situations until you are in them. But don’t doubt that you are capable. You are not the body, and you are not the mind’s reactions to what is happening. You are the one who is aware of all of it. Just like a light shining on an object doesn’t break when the object breaks, your consciousness remains untouched by the events happening around you. The more you meditate and work on letting go, the more you will come to know this directly—not as a belief, but as a reality you have lived.

Look at the great beings who have walked this earth—people like Gandhi. He was shot while giving a peaceful speech, and as he fell to the ground, he bowed in forgiveness. It is possible to be so free inside that even in the most extreme moments, there is peace. That’s not just an idea—it’s a state of being that a human being can reach. Will you reach that state? Who knows? But don’t assume you can’t. The depth of who you are is beyond anything the mind can comprehend.

When life challenges you, meet it with openness. If it is time to act, act with clarity. If there is nothing you can do, then surrender fully, knowing that your growth is happening in real time. You will find that even in the most difficult moments, there is a space inside of you that remains untouched. That space is where true peace lies.

7-2.q: Why do we store bad experiences, and how can we let them go?
7-2.a:
When an experience happens, it should naturally move through you and get stored in your long-term memory, just like a computer saves data. But sometimes, you don’t store it cleanly. Instead, you resist the experience, or you cling to it, and that resistance or attachment keeps it from passing all the way through. Now, instead of just being a memory, it becomes something more—it carries emotional weight, and it stays active inside of you. That’s what a samskara is: an impression that didn’t get stored properly because you either didn’t like the experience or liked it too much and didn’t want to lose it.

This is why certain experiences seem to keep coming back up on their own. You don’t try to remember every random moment of your life, but the ones you resisted, the ones that weren’t stored cleanly, those are the ones that keep resurfacing. It’s like they’re sitting right in front of you, ready to jump back into your awareness at any moment. You could be walking down a street that has nothing to do with the past event, and suddenly—there it is again. That’s because you stored it with disturbance instead of neutrality.

How do you let it go? You neutralize it as it arises. When one of these experiences resurfaces, don’t resist. Don’t push it away or judge it. Just relax

Resistance and Acceptance 	63

while you let it come up. Let the experience come and go without grabbing on to it, the same way you’d let a passing breeze move through an open window. Over time, if you keep relaxing and not fueling the past impression with more resistance, it will lose its charge. It will simply become a clean memory, like everything else you’ve experienced but don’t obsess over.

Your past doesn’t have to control you. What happened, happened. Life includes all kinds of experiences—some pleasant, some painful. You don’t have to let them run your life. If you stop resisting, stop holding on to them, they will pass through you, and you will be free.

7-3.q: Can avoiding difficult situations, instead of having to resist them, be helpful for your spiritual growth?
7-3.a:
When you remove yourself from the noise and complexity of the world, there will be fewer things triggering your inner disturbances. Don’t mistake that for spiritual growth. You have to understand—peace is not the absence of disturbing situations; it’s the ability to remain undisturbed regardless of the situation. If you run away from the world thinking that isolation will free you, you’ll find that the mind still finds things to resist. You’ll hear a dog barking in the quiet woods, and suddenly, that’s the problem. If you are still reacting, then you haven’t solved anything—you’ve just changed the scenery.

The real work is not about avoiding difficult situations; it’s about letting go of what gets triggered inside you. You can’t grow spiritually by running from what challenges you. You grow by using every situation—whether it’s the chaos of a busy city or the solitude of the forest—as an opportunity to let go of the personal mind’s reactions. When something disturbs you, that’s life showing you exactly where your work is. If you remove yourself from people because they trigger you, then all you’ve done is delay the inevitable. Eventually, something else will take their place. The only way to truly free yourself is to stop running and start releasing.

Retreating can be helpful, but it’s not the whole answer. If you take a break to center yourself, to quiet down and gain clarity, that’s fine. But don’t think that quieting the external world is the same as quieting the inner one. At some point, you will have to return and face life. The real test is whether you can stand in the middle of New York City, surrounded by noise and chaos, and still feel completely at peace—not because the world changed, but because you did.

Instead of hiding from the things that stir you up, welcome them. When life triggers something inside you, say, “Thank you. Thank you for showing me something I need to let go of.” If your goal is to rise beyond the mind’s limitations, you don’t want to avoid your stuff—you want to be free of it. Freedom only comes when you are no longer controlled by what disturbs you. Let go, surrender, and watch as your consciousness naturally rises. The peace you seek is already inside you—it’s just buried beneath all the things you refuse to release.

7-4.q: Can the practice of acceptance help one heal physically and emotionally when faced with illness?
7-4.a:
When it comes to healing, the first thing you have to do is accept what is happening. If you resist, you block the natural flow of energy, and that very resistance creates even more tension and suffering. Healing is not just a physical process—it is deeply tied to your inner state. If you fight against what’s happening, you end up with both a struggling body and a struggling mind. Start by accepting that this is what is happening right now, and it’s okay. That doesn’t mean you don’t take action; you still do what is necessary to seek the best care available. But you stop fighting the reality of the situation within yourself.

Once you stop resisting, you allow the natural intelligence of life to flow through you. Healing is not something you control—it is something you allow. Just like your body has an immune system that knows how to fight off illness, your inner being has a way of working through pain when you don’t interfere. Think about how some people in hospitals heal faster simply because they have the love and support of family and friends around them. That uplifted energy makes a difference. When you relax and open, you create space for that healing energy to do its work.

You also should be willing to find something positive about what you’re going through. No matter what is happening, there is always an opportunity for growth. Maybe this experience is teaching you patience, surrender, or

Resistance and Acceptance 	65

trust. Maybe it’s showing you how much support and love are actually around you. Look for what life is giving you through this, rather than only seeing what it seems to be taking away. This shift in perspective changes everything.

So don’t resist. Do what is necessary, but keep your heart open. The energy of healing is always trying to move through you—you just have to let it.

7-5.q: I’ve experienced chronic pain for many years. How do I work with illness and pain in the physical body as part of my spiritual practice?
7-5.a:
Chronic illness and its accompanying physical pain is a different experience than the inner discomfort of mental and emotional purification. However, from a spiritual perspective, they are dealt with similarly. Obviously, if you are ill, you do what you can medically to correct the problem causing the pain. Unfortunately, that does not always work. If you are left with physical pain you simply have to live with, you deal with that by letting go. After all, you really have no choice—it’s either accept or resist, and resistance makes the physical pain worse, due to the tension it creates in the body. Resistance also causes a disturbed mind and uncomfortable emotions. Now you have two problems—outside and inside. It is important to come to peace inwardly and not allow the state of the body to determine the quality of your inner life.

Acceptance means you do your best to relax through the pain. Just like when doing a yoga asana, you relax through any tension. It is not easy or pleasant, but in time, you learn to transcend the intensity of the physical discomfort. Next, you always pay attention to what part of you is experiencing the pain. You are witnessing that the body feels pain, but who are you back in there aware that the body is sending you these messages? The Self, the awareness of being, has no pain—it is experiencing the pain that the body is generating. If you can relax and center on who’s aware of the pain, instead of getting lost in it, you can actually use the pain to free yourself.

Obviously, nobody said this is going to be easy. But since you asked how to deal with chronic pain spiritually, this is the answer—use it for self-realization.

7-6.q: Is it normal to feel constant stress even while relaxing and releasing? I want to make sure I am not suppressing instead of actually letting go.
7-6.a:
It is important to understand that while we are growing, situations will arise that are difficult for us to accept. During these situations, we have the tendency to resist. Resistance causes physical, emotional, and mental stress. What can we do about this?

The answer is to relax. Relaxation is the opposite of stress. If you do your best to relax when you feel the tendency to resist and close, over time you will find this reduces your level of stress about the situation. When you deeply relax inside, you will be able to lean away from the inner energy that you are wanting to resist. It’s not easy, but once you are committed to relaxing instead of resisting, you will feel a separation between your sense of awareness and the energy trying to pass through. You will clearly see that you are not comfortable with this energy and that is why you are almost instinctually resisting it. Once you achieve this separation between your awareness and the energy coming at you, you will have an opportunity to lean away from the energy and let it pass by.

As an analogy, let’s say you are facing a strong wind blowing in your face. You don’t like it, so you pick up a sheet of plywood and hold it up against the wind to protect yourself. That will create tremendous stress trying to fight the wind. You do have another choice for how to deal with the wind in your face: you can let down the plywood, relax, lean backwards, and allow the wind to blow past you. That is what is meant by not resisting the force that is trying to pass through—just let it pass.

This is a very high technique for releasing blockages. Don’t feel that you should be able to succeed at this right away or under all circumstances. It takes practice with lots of low-hanging fruit in order to develop the ability to do this under strong winds. But every little effort moves you in the right direction. Just do your best to let go instead of resisting, and you will be growing spiritually.

8-1.q: Are acceptance and surrender the same thing?
8-1.a:
Your question is very deep. The simplest answer would be yes: acceptance and surrender are the same thing. But there really is an important difference. If an event happens and you feel resistance to it, you can simply tell yourself to accept it because it is out of your control. That is acceptance. If it is a major event, like your partner leaving you, you will go through a lot of pain in your heart, but ultimately you will have to accept that the relationship is over.

Surrender goes much deeper. Surrender means not only accepting the pain of the situation, but also releasing the root cause of your resistance— the underlying samskara. If you are to surrender to the experience of your partner leaving you, you are not just letting go of the relationship (as if you have a choice); you are also surrendering the part of you that wants to resist. Acceptance says, “I want to resist, but I will not express that outwardly. I will accept the reality of the situation.” Surrender says, “I want to let go of any part of me that wants to resist. My life is about letting go of what I am watching inside myself, not just letting go of what is happening outside.”

In the end, acceptance can be a strictly mental rationalization process. But surrender is the indwelling witness willingly letting go of what is pulling it into inner turmoil. It is the Self relaxing and releasing through all that is happening inside. Acceptance makes life more tolerable; surrender makes life a spiritual experience. I hope this helps you learn to let go at the deepest levels.

8-2.q: How can I practice surrender when faced with personal struggles and negativity?
8-2.a:
When you talk about surrender, understand that you’re not surrendering to some external force or giving up on life. You’re surrendering the part of you that is struggling—the part of your mind that is constantly trying to control everything to be the way it wants. That mind is always disturbed about one thing or another. It holds on to past painful experiences and reacts to life based on those impressions. If it truly knew what to do to end its suffering, it would just do it. Real surrender means letting go of that part of you and allowing something greater to guide you.

Look at the deepest spiritual beings throughout time—the ones who have merged completely into the flow of life and found the deepest peace. They didn’t get there by controlling everything; they got there by releasing themselves into something much bigger than their personal mind. They let go; they allowed life to unfold as it naturally does, and in doing so, they merged with the great oneness that is always there. You don’t have to fight with life. You don’t have to resist what’s happening. You simply need to step back, watch your mind trying to grasp for control, and say to it, “It’s okay. You don’t have to do this anymore.”

That’s what true surrender is. It’s the willingness to let go of the struggle to make everything be the way you think it should be, and instead, trust life. Not in a passive way, not in a way where you do nothing, but in a way where you stop interfering with the natural flow of life. The more you let go, the more you’ll feel a deep sense of peace arising within you. At some point, you will realize this peace has always been there—it was just buried under all the resistance.



When you’re faced with personal struggles and negativity arises, don’t suppress it and don’t fight it. Just step back, watch it, and let it pass through. You are not your thoughts. You are not your emotions. You are the one who is aware of them. The deeper you go into that awareness, the more you will understand what it truly means to surrender.

8-3.q: If someone at work bullies me, does surrender mean I just let it happen? Is speaking up for myself or avoiding them outside of work a form of suppression?
8-3.a:
The teachings of surrender are not about letting yourself become a doormat for the inappropriate behavior of others. Surrender is about letting go of your reactive response and then dealing with things from a place of clarity and logic. It’s all about your intent. If you are letting go sincerely, and circumstances are such that you need to assert yourself with your coworker, first let go of your reactive energies, then interact from a place of clarity. This is not suppression.

Choosing not to interact with a coworker outside of your work assignments is not suppression either. But if you are avoiding someone because you can’t handle how they make you feel inside, then work on yourself to let go so that you aren’t avoiding out of reaction. If you choose to avoid them, let it be out of sincerely seeking the best overall solution to the situation. This is not setting personal boundaries, which is just protecting your ego; it is consciously working to bring the highest peace possible for both parties.

8-4.q: How do I know when to act in a situation and when to surrender action? In The Surrender Experiment, you fought having a construction dump built in your neighborhood. How did you know that you should act to stop it?
8-4.a:
Your question is very beautiful and is one that many people struggle with, because the teaching is so subtle. When you walk the path of surrender, it will look as though you are living in the world and acting out of the same motivations as others. But the motivation is not the same, because you are not trying to get something or avoid something; you are trying to be a servant of the situation.

When you let go of your personal preferences, that doesn’t mean you won’t end up having a role to play in a situation. The difference is that you first let go of your personal reactions, then simply listen to life for guidance on whether there is anything you can do to serve. You then follow life’s flow and participate. In this way, your participation is not motivated by personal preference, but by the intention to intelligently serve the situation and raise it to the highest possible level.

In the case of the garbage dump, it was a matter of letting go of preferences and listening to life for guidance. Because the Temple was the largest landowner in the area, all the neighbors were asking the Temple for help to stop the dump. We served the situation to the best of our ability. And because we were willing to play the role life gave us with impersonal clarity, life was able to unfold to the amazing results you read about in the book.

When you are present and open, life unfolds, and you will naturally have a role to serve it, rather than trying to make it serve you. You become a servant of the present moment, and your only goal is to make sure that every moment that passes before you is better off because it did.

8-5.q: I want to live in accordance with The Surrender Experiment. But I can’t say yes to every opportunity—there are too many. How do I choose without relying on my personal preferences?
8-5.a:
Surrender is a very deep subject, and it is something that matures as you practice. Surrender is not about doing or not doing—it is about letting go of the lower aspects of yourself.

Behind everything we do, there are motives. Some are normal physiological drives for food, clothing, and shelter. But nowadays, most of our motives are psychologically based. “I’m lonely, I want to find someone.” “I feel awkward, I want to feel more self-confident.” “I need more money so that I can do the things that I like.” These are not necessities; they are attempts to compensate for the psychological lack we feel inside. There is nothing inherently wrong with this, but it limits us to a life of struggling to be okay. If you are working for the part of your being that is not well, you will never really get free. There will always be something inside that is bothering you.

In a nutshell, surrender means letting go of that personal part of your being, instead of serving it. You set a higher motive than just trying to be okay. Serving others is a higher motive, but you can’t really devote yourself to serving if you are constantly bothered by a sense of lack inside. So, you decide to devote your life to letting go of your lower self in order to experience and express a higher part of your being. You look and see where you are coming from and try to come from the highest place you can see. If you do this constantly, with everything, little by little you will find the beauty and greatness of freeing yourself from yourself. Once the lower, personal, psychological motives fall off, what is left is a very great being, filled with love, joy, and constant inspiration and clarity.

What about all these opportunities that are presenting themselves to you? Instead of getting stressed about choices, try to be aware of the underlying motives that are causing all the stress. Fear of loss and desire for gain cause quite a commotion inside. Once you can stand in the midst of the everchanging world passing before you, and remain centered, quiet, and still, you will see a path that looks higher and purer than the rest. Follow that, and don’t think about the choice ever again. Make it the right choice by doing your best and never second-guessing yourself. Fully embrace and honor the results that follow—learn from them and grow into something great. This is how a great person lives, and simply living such a life leads to the highest state, outside and in. And remember: everything is fine, as long as you are fine within.

8-6.q: How can I tell if the urge to create is coming from an ego-driven desire or a state of surrender to something greater?
8-6.a:
To know if the urge to create is coming from ego or something spiritual, you need to look deeply at what’s actually happening inside of you. You are not just some small person trying to make things happen—you are the conscious awareness watching all of this. And that same conscious awareness is the creative force behind the entire universe. What gets in the way is the personal self—the ego. If you’re creating because you want something for yourself, to build an identity and get recognition, then that is ego. That’s you trying to manipulate life to fit your personal desires.

In contrast, if you don’t let your personal thoughts and emotions interfere, the creative force will still flow, but now it won’t be about you. It will simply be an expression of the energy of life itself. The problem is that most people don’t trust life enough to let it happen that way. Instead, they grasp at things, try to control outcomes, and get attached to what they create. That’s when the ego takes something natural and turns it into something personal. You have to be very honest with yourself: Are you creating because something is naturally flowing through you, or because you are trying to make something happen for yourself?

If you truly let go, then creativity will happen—but it won’t be for you. It will simply be the divine energy moving through an open channel. Ironically, when you stop trying to create for ego, what comes through is far more beautiful and powerful than anything you could have come up with by yourself. Your only job is to step aside. You’re going to see that creative expression doesn’t need you in order to happen. It’s already happening outside and in. You just need to stop blocking it.

8-7.q: In your life of surrender, what role did trust play?
8-7.a:
Let me explain trust differently than we normally think of it. To begin with, trust is not simply about trusting people you’re interacting with. When you do that, what you’re really doing is trusting they will behave the way you expect, and that is your ego protecting itself. Real trust is at a much deeper level.

Spiritually, there are two fundamental types of trust. First, the trust that life will unfold exactly as it’s meant to, not according to your will, but according to all the forces that create reality. Second, the trust that no matter what happens, you will be able to handle it. Those are the kinds of trust that define your life. They go far beyond simply trusting individuals to act a certain way. Because, as life has shown all of us, sometimes people do not act as expected. Trusting people to act a certain way is conditional trust. Unconditional trust is at a whole other level, and it leads to the peace that passeth all understanding.

8-8.q: When is it appropriate to take action in difficult situations, as opposed to letting go?
8-8.a:
Choosing whether to take action in a difficult situation requires first asking yourself whether there is anything personal involved. You can always tell the difference between personal and impersonal. If there’s any sense of “I,” “me,” or “mine” in what you’re about to do, or if you’re thinking things like, I don’t like what they said to me, and I need to make sure they understand why, then it’s personal. If it’s personal, it means you are acting from a place of ego, and that’s exactly what you’re trying to let go of.

Your mind will try to justify action in these moments by saying it’s for the good of the situation or the other person. You have to be brutally honest with yourself—are you really acting for the benefit of the situation, or are you acting for yourself? Are you trying to fix something outside so you don’t have to feel uncomfortable inside? If you are, then the answer is simple: let go. Use that moment to release the part of you that wants to control, defend, or prove something. You don’t suppress ego, and you don’t push it away—you simply relax and let it pass through you.

Letting go doesn’t mean there aren’t times to act. You just don’t act from personal reaction. You wait until you have let go of yourself by relaxing behind your inner disturbance. When you are truly quiet inside—when your sense of “I” has relaxed—then and only then can you look at the situation with clarity. In that clarity, you ask, “Is there something I can do here that would serve the moment, not serve me?” Most of the time, when you get to this place, you’ll find there is nothing you need to do. The whole situation resolves itself simply because you are no longer caught up in it.

Sometimes, however, you may find there is a right action to take—not because you need to take it, but because the moment calls for it. When action comes from that place, and is simply the natural flow of the situation, it is effortless. There is no struggle, no resistance, no personal agenda. That is the difference between true right action and reaction. One is born from surrender, the other from resistance. Your entire spiritual path is about learning to let go of resistance. Do it moment by moment, situation by situation, until there is nothing left inside of you that needs the world to be a certain way for you to be okay. You are free inside, and your simple presence serves to set others free.

8-9.q: You teach that when we let go and surrender, we will feel bliss all the time. How can I be in bliss if someone I love is ill?
8-9.a:
Surrender does not mean that when something sad or painful is happening, you will feel happy. Let’s take an example of having a child with a serious illness. Of course, if your child is very ill, you won’t be laughing and experiencing happiness. It is natural to feel deep pain and concern. The key is to not resist your feelings regarding the situation. Surrender means that you are able to accept the situation as reality and then deal with it from a place of clarity. You cannot help your child or raise the situation if you are not able to accept what is happening.

The work is to let go of your own inner resistance and be willing to experience the natural sadness, fear, and other very human emotions that will arise. Then serve the situation as best as you can to help raise it. This leaves you clear to love your child and compassionately support them through the reality of a difficult illness. The deep growth that comes from letting go at this level will increase your capacity to love and serve in this world. Surrender is a very deep practice. By accepting reality, you discover the beauty and growth to be found in all experiences.

8-10.q: What is the highest form of surrender?
8-10.a:
The highest form of surrender is realizing that the universe is already perfect, unfolding with a divine intelligence beyond anything the mind can comprehend. Yet all we do is get in its way. Our job is not to control life or manifest things according to our personal desires, but to step aside and allow the universal perfection to express itself. True surrender is not about creating outcomes; it’s about dissolving the part of our being that thinks it needs to.

When you let go, the energy of life—shakti—moves freely, and what is meant to be can unfold. This is not about using surrender as a strategy to get what you want. That’s not surrender; that’s still ego. Real surrender is when you are willing to completely let go of you—in other words, to die to be reborn. It’s when you stop using life to get what you want and instead allow life to strip you of everything false so that only truth remains.

How deep do you want to go? Surrender doesn’t mean that only good things will happen to you. That’s still ego, holding on to control. Real surrender is when you let go so completely that whatever happens—whether pleasant or painful—is just another step toward dissolving the personal self. Every moment is presenting you with opportunities to let go. The more you surrender, the more space there is for God, for truth, for the unfolding of the divine. That is the highest state. That is what surrender is all about.

9-1.q: A major technique in The Untethered Soul is learning to let go. Do any of your teachings give a simple description of how to implement this practice?
9-1.a:
Letting go is simply the act of relaxing in the face of your inner reactive energy and then leaning back, away from the pull of the reaction. The tendency is to come forward and deal with the disturbance. Instead, just relax your shoulders, relax your heart, and relax your abdominal area. You do this instead of engaging with the thoughts and emotions.

If you do this, you will see that the distance between you and the reaction increases, and you will find yourself farther back behind it all. You will still feel the pull of the reaction’s energy, but you will learn to relax and lean away from that pull. Keep in mind these are just words trying to describe the inner experience of letting go. Once you practice this and see the shift in your position in relation to the reactive energy, you can use your own words.



Perhaps this will help: don’t use will to resist the energy coming up; use it to relax and allow the energy to pass.

Do your best every single day. Don’t judge the process; just trust that by letting go, you are welcoming the release of the disturbances you’ve stored inside. If you do this constantly, one day you will notice a beautiful energy flow within you. Just keep letting go, and eventually the energy flow will feed you day and night, and you will live in a state of constant joy, love, and ecstasy.

9-2.q: I try to relax when uncomfortable feelings arise and remind myself to let them go. Is there some clear way to be sure that I have let go correctly instead of suppressing?
9-2.a:
There is no “correctly” when it comes to things like letting go. There is only sincerity of intent. If your intent is to relax, let go, and not push discomfort back down, then you are not suppressing. Ego reactions have been down there for a long time; they are not going to go away immediately. The shakti will push up that which you need to deal with at any given moment. Your only job is to intend to let it go and not protect yourself by pushing the difficult feelings away. Anything you can do to keep from pushing the feelings back down is fine. Affirmation, mantra, and the practice of witness consciousness are all appropriate and very helpful in the long run.

Offering your stuff up to the vast Universe, to God, is also a wonderful practice. Offering up is the opposite of pushing back down. Make it a fun game. Enjoy the process of letting go of uncomfortable thoughts and emotions. You don’t want them in there, so when they come up, relax and release to the best of your ability. Don’t let your mind create a preconceived notion of what letting go is supposed to feel like. Just keep relaxing and releasing. Everything will unfold in its own time. Your job is to stay out of the way. Just relax your heart and stay behind the mind. Breathe slowly and deeply when things get really tough. When your sincere intent is to let go, everything helps, and all of life is your path Home.

9-3.q: I would really appreciate if you could give me a tip on how to completely release blockages from my life.
9-3.a:
The most helpful tip to enable you to completely release things you are holding on to is to start with small things. Let go of the meaningless stuff that upsets you, like when you’ve misplaced something, or someone is driving too slow in front of you, or you don’t like the weather. Practice relaxing and let the annoyances pass through. Notice you are the one that is noticing the disturbance—you are not the disturbance itself. Just relax and let it go. Every single day, practice letting go with the small stuff that bothers you. If you do this, you will find that the more difficult things you’ve been holding on to will begin to release.

How will you know it is working? You’ll begin to notice that things that used to disturb you no longer do so. Because you’ve become accustomed to releasing inner disturbance, what used to seem so big will begin to feel more like the small stuff. Over time, because you are no longer holding on to disturbance, you will naturally begin to feel more love and openness within.

9-4.q: I struggle with consistently letting go. I’ve tried both actively letting go and simply allowing things to happen, but sometimes it doesn’t seem to work. I’m not sure I’m doing it correctly.
9-4.a:
Thank you for sharing your experience of letting go. To begin with, there is no such thing as “letting go doesn’t work.” You just can’t see the results right away.

When you are learning a sport or how to play an instrument, you know it’s not going to happen right away. It takes practice under varying conditions. Perhaps in tennis your forehand is good, but your backhand is weak. Every time you practice your backhand, even if the ball goes into the net, you are improving. Every single ball you hit makes your wrists and arms stronger and improves your hand-eye coordination. Practice makes perfect.

The same is true for letting go. Events in the world hit our stuff inside, and this causes discomfort and resistance. If you go with those reactions, you are protecting the very samskaras that got hit. If you endeavor to relax in the face of the inner disturbance, you are allowing room for release of the blocked energies from the past. They will not all pass through right away, and of course you don’t feel an upward shift in energy every time you try to let things go. But over time, you will become a more open person, and events will more naturally pass through. Once you become good at letting go of the little everyday situations that disturb you, you will see that larger things from the past can be released when they come up.

Let your intent be to relentlessly let go of whatever hits your stored blockages. Then give the blockages the room they need to release. You do this by constantly relaxing behind the reactive disturbed energies that get created inside. If you do your best at this, and that is by definition the best you can do, you will grow every day. Don’t judge the process; just trust that by letting go, you are welcoming the release of what is blocked inside. When enough has been released, you will start to feel the upward flow of the shakti lifting you into a state of unconditional well-being.

9-5.q: Once we have acknowledged a painful feeling and have relaxed and released, can we shift our attention to something else, or do we have to stay with it until it dissolves?
9-5.a:
When you have deeply acknowledged a painful feeling, relaxed around it, and done your best to release any resistance you have toward it, then, yes, you go about your business with daily tasks. You don’t have to stay focused on it. Just understand that while you are going about your business, if the feeling comes up strongly again, you should stop for a moment and deeply relax and release, just as you did before. Do this as many times as you need to so that the energy can be released, instead of being suppressed again.

What you don’t want to do is push the painful feeling back down because you can’t handle it coming up. Always welcome it coming up, and try to be comfortable behind the uncomfortable feeling. You don’t have to be fixated on the painful feeling; that does not help it pass. Try to go about your business while giving it the right to release naturally. If you have some time to be alone with it, deeply relax around it with a sense that the fire you are experiencing is the fire of purification. Learn to love that fire—it will free you over time.

9-6.q: I have been practicing the teachings for a few years, and they have definitely been working. But some of my blockages seem to keep coming back—what am I doing wrong?
9-6.a:
You are doing very well to be willing to look inside and see the blockages that continue to persist. Rather than getting down on yourself, understand that some blockages have been down there a long time, and they will take time to release. Start from where you are, and work on letting go every day. If you forget, don’t get discouraged. The minute you see you got lost in negativity, pick yourself back up and let go. Let the path unfold in its own time and let it be an amazing, exciting journey to inner liberation.

One should not think they can learn to do this all at once. It takes time and relentless practice to be able to let go. You start with small things, like the mind’s complaints about the weather, or getting uptight about the driver in front of you. Just relax your way through the disturbances the mind and heart are creating. Little by little, it becomes natural to let go instead of causing yourself grief over meaningless things. You will then be able to handle larger disturbances, and eventually you will be able to handle any disturbance. In the end, you will be free of disturbance—even though disturbances can still happen.

Along the way, there are many stages you will go through as the deeper blockages start to release. It is not unusual to go through periods of darkness while the blockages are moving around down there, blocking the energy flow. It’s not easy, but the highest technique is to relax behind the darkness, behind the discomfort. Who notices the pit in your stomach? How do you know it’s there? Because you are the consciousness experiencing that knot in your stomach. You are not the knot; you are the conscious experiencer of the knot. Be that consciousness and relax. This allows the blockage the room it needs to release. The stuff down there was stored with pain, and it is going to release with pain. Be glad it is coming up; you do not want to live with it for the rest of your life. Be positive about the cleansing. Reach down, scoop up a handful, and offer it to the vast Universe—to God. Let your mantra be, I can handle this. I can handle this. Then relax and relax again. If you do this, the transformation will happen naturally, over time.

9-7.q: Will letting go address long-held internal blocks that have become part of your self-concept?
9-7.a:
If you sincerely want to free yourself from the burdens of your past conditioning, the answer is simple: let go. No matter how long you’ve carried something inside you—whether it’s an old blockage, a belief, or part of your selfconcept—if you stop resisting, it will pass through and leave you in a higher state. The only reason these things stay with you is because you’re holding on to them. You may not realize it, but deep inside, there’s a resistance, a pushing away. That very resistance is what keeps your blockages stored inside.

Look at how the body works. It has an immune system that knows how to heal. If something unhealthy enters, your body does everything in its power to expel it. Your mind works the same way. The reason these old patterns keep surfacing isn’t because they’re meant to stay with you forever—it’s because they’re trying to release. But instead of letting them go, what do you do? You push them back down. You get scared and uncomfortable, so you suppress them again, or defend yourself from what caused them to come up. Don’t do that. When something arises inside of you, ask yourself a simple question: “Do I want this in there?” If the answer is no, then stop holding on to it.

The truth is, nothing is glued inside of you. There is no flypaper, no superglue—it’s just your own will resisting. When something comes up, just relax. Breathe. Let it have space to pass through. This isn’t about fighting with your mind or forcing things away. You’re not trying to get rid of anything; you’re simply letting go of what is already trying to leave. When the pain arises, don’t engage with it, don’t analyze it, and don’t argue with it. Just relax and let it pass. You are not the pain—you are the one who is aware of it. The moment you stop resisting, you’ll see how naturally it fades away.

Letting go is not complicated. It’s just that you’ve spent your whole life doing the opposite. You’ve been taught to grab on to things, to build an identity around your thoughts and emotions. You don’t need to do that anymore. You are a free being—all that’s left is to let go of the noisy mind that tells you otherwise.

9-8.q: How can I tell the difference between surrendering my inner disturbances and suppressing them?
9-8.a:
If you are uncomfortable experiencing what your mind or emotions are doing, the tendency is to do something about it. You want to do something that makes it more tolerable. That tendency is at the root of suppression. Because you don’t want to experience what is before you, you either push it away (suppression) or use the mind to create thoughts that make it feel better (rationalization). This is dangerous territory, because if you push an experience away now, you will have to keep pushing it away for the rest of your life. It will still be in there, and external events and inner thought patterns will stimulate it to come back up. And even when it’s not consciously bothering you, it will be blocking your energy flow. In a similar way, while rationalization can be used to offset difficult feelings, which is better than pushing them away, it leaves you responsible for making sure your rationalizations can withstand the challenges of the real world.

The alternative to all this struggling and long-term suffering is the practice of letting go. You return to the root of the problem: the tendency to resist the mental and emotional disturbances. Thoughts cannot hurt you—they are just thoughts. Emotions cannot hurt you—they are just emotions. It is your resistance to them that causes the problem. Similarly, within reason, wind cannot hurt you. It just blows past you. But if you can’t handle that experience, you’ll have to buy a 4x8-foot sheet of plywood and hold it up to block the wind. Good luck! Your arms will become tired, and your whole life will be determined by your inability to handle the wind blowing across your face. It is exactly the same with thoughts and emotions. They are passing before you, and if you can let them be, they will pass in their own time. Handled this way, they do not leave scars that burden you for life. They are gone, just like every other event in life comes and goes. That is letting go, and it is totally different from suppression and rationalization. The problem is, we haven’t learned how to do it.

The key to letting go is to relax in the face of discomfort. Don’t try to make the mind or emotions not feel disturbed. Letting go is not about the disturbance itself—it is about you in there, the one that is experiencing the disturbance. You relax. Relax in the face of the disturbance, just as you relax in the face of the wind. No resistance; just deep relaxation. People don’t want to do this—they want to fix the disturbance. But letting go allows the space necessary for the energy of the disturbance to pass through without getting stuck inside. Plus, it simultaneously allows the samskara that caused the disturbance to release. This is what it means to let go.

9-9.q: I have been practicing letting go, but how do I know if the technique is truly working? I feel better momentarily, but my blockages seem to return. I’m having trouble staying motivated.
9-9.a:
Thank you for sending your sincere question. There are a number of ways to see that the process is working. First, imagine if you didn’t let go of things as they happen—these lower energies would run your life. That is one immediate benefit: you don’t allow the lower blockages to completely take over and mess up your external life. It is like breaking a habit—if you repeat the habit every time you have the urge, you are reinforcing the behavior pattern. If you bother to withstand the urge, you are working on breaking the habit.

The same is true with your inner psychological habit patterns. If you give in to them, you reinforce them, and they will become stronger. If you try to release them, over time their energy will be rerouted and transmuted. This is the second benefit: you are rerouting energy patterns instead of reinforcing them. Over time, enough energy will be released to flow upward, and you will begin to notice you are happier and less reactive.

If you keep letting go, the upward flow will become stronger and stronger until it is a major force in your daily life. If you ask how long this will take—it’s none of your business! This is a natural process of purification, and the only reason it takes any time is because you are holding on to and supporting the inner blockages. You must learn over time, through daily experiences, to realize you don’t have to hold on to everything that ever bothered you in the past (including five minutes ago!).

Do your work of letting go to the best of your ability—the rest will take care of itself. When you do this inner work, you are carrying out the purpose of your life, and all of life will support you. But not necessarily in the ways you expect. This is where true surrender comes in—you do the work and allow the infinite force that created the universe to do the rest.

9-10.q: Can loving and thanking inner demons or past struggles be part of letting go?
9-10.a:
If something from your past comes up—old pain, struggles, things you once saw as demons—don’t push it away. Don’t fight with it. Instead, love it to death. Do you understand how powerful that is? If you love what comes up from your past, you’re not resisting it. You’re not suppressing it. You’re allowing it to come up, be released, and finally pass through.

This is not about pretending the event didn’t happen or trying to make it something it’s not. It’s about honoring it for the growth it gave you. Every single thing that has ever happened to you, no matter how difficult, has shaped you. It has helped you learn and brought you to this exact moment. Instead of holding it in as some kind of burden, thank it and let it go.

Letting go is not an act of rejection—it’s an act of deep acceptance. You’re not saying, “This should not have happened.” You’re saying, “It did happen, and I am at peace with it.” This applies to your past relationships, mistakes, and your so-called failures. You should be able to look back and say, “That helped me. That taught me. That made me who I am today.” If you can do that with an open heart, you’ll see that you don’t need to carry any of it as a weight anymore. You honor it, and in that honoring, it dissolves. That’s real letting go, and that’s how you become free.

10-1.q: How can I avoid adapting my life to fit my internal problems?
10-1.a:
You are correct; your life isn’t supposed to be structured around protecting your issues and making sure they never get triggered. That’s what the mind does—it builds walls, makes excuses, and rearranges the world to avoid discomfort. That’s not freedom. That’s a prison.

Your life has meaning because you are letting go of the lower aspects of yourself. The whole process of life—of creation itself—is designed to help you evolve into a higher state of being. You can’t do that if you keep adjusting your life to accommodate your fears and insecurities. If you have blockages inside, don’t protect them—release them. Life will bring you everything you need for your spiritual growth. You don’t have to force it or even understand it. Just stop resisting.

10-2.q: Why does the process of spiritual growth often involve discomfort or pain?
10-2.a:
If it was stored with pain, it is going to release with pain. You have stored blockages inside of you which are restricting your natural energy flow. Life is constantly trying to bring those blockages up so they can be released. Instead of letting them go, you resist. You don’t want to feel insecurity, fear, or loss, so you try to manipulate the world around you to keep those feelings buried. But life won’t let you do that forever. Life is designed to help you evolve, and that means it’s going to bring up everything inside of you that needs to be purified.

When you feel emotional pain, it’s because energy that was supposed to flow freely is now hitting resistance. Maybe you built your sense of self around a relationship, a job, or an idea of how life should be, and then something happens to shake that foundation. It feels like your heart is on fire because the energy cannot flow around your blockages anymore and is bouncing back inside you. Instead of fighting, what if you saw that discomfort as an opportunity? What if, instead of pushing it away, you let it burn through whatever is in the way? That’s real growth.

Spiritual growth isn’t about protecting yourself from pain; it’s about letting go of the part of you that gets disturbed. A truly free being doesn’t need life to be a certain way to feel okay. They don’t hold on to the past, they don’t resist the present, and they don’t live in fear of the future. They let go and allow the natural energy of life to flow unimpeded. That’s what liberation is.

Don’t be afraid of discomfort. Welcome it. When life shakes you, see it as an invitation to release what’s holding you back. The more you let go, the more the beautiful energy inside you will rise, and one day, there won’t be pain anymore—there will be freedom.

10-3.q: Why does my ego resist so strongly when I try to stay centered and let go?
10-3.a:
