The moment you take on that role, you’ve made it about you—about your need for them to be your way, about your discomfort with how they are. That’s not love, and it’s certainly not surrender. Instead of focusing on whether they are growing the way you think they should, turn inward. Use the relationship as a way to let go of yourself, to release whatever is causing your frustration.

Your responsibility in a relationship is not to impose your spiritual path onto someone else. It’s to bring the highest version of yourself into the relationship. Be a source of love, of kindness, of unwavering presence. If you can show up with deep acceptance and embody peace instead of preaching it, that alone will do more to inspire change than any teaching can. People don’t change because you tell them to; they change because they feel something in you that touches them at a deeper level.

What if they never change? Then that’s reality, and your work is to accept it. A true spiritual path isn’t about controlling the outside world—it’s about learning to be okay with exactly what is. If your partner comes to you and asks for guidance, by all means, share it. If they don’t, your role is to love them as they are, without judgment, resistance, or frustration. The moment you stop needing them to be different, you’ll find that your disturbance disappears on its own.

Spiritual growth isn’t about others. It’s about you. If you feel frustrated because someone else isn’t growing the way you want, that’s your work. That’s what you need to let go of. Use the relationship for your own growth—release your expectations, surrender your resistance, and bring the highest version of yourself into every moment. Allow life to take care of the rest. That is the greatest gift you can offer, both to your partner and to yourself.

14-6.q: How can I respond to people who think spiritual growth requires worldly success first?
14-6.a:
If someone believes that worldly success must come before spiritual growth, you don’t need to argue with them. You can simply say, “That’s beautiful.” It’s beautiful that they have aspirations, that they believe certain things will help them on their path. That’s where you leave it. Let them find out for themselves. There is nothing you can say to talk them out of the stage they’re in. Everyone moves through life in their own way, at their own pace. If you want to help, begin by honoring that truth.

Ultimately, the most powerful thing you can do is to live the teachings. If you carry yourself with peace, with clarity, with inner joy, it will have an effect on others. Over time, they will see that you have changed, that you are centered in a way that has nothing to do with external success. That’s the real teaching—not words, but the way you live.

Great masters understand this. When someone comes to them and says, “I feel like I need success, I need pleasure, I need to explore life in this way,” the response isn’t to correct that person or to try to stop them. Instead, it’s to say, “That’s beautiful. If that’s what you need, then go through it. Just take God with you.” Whatever you do, bring awareness, bring presence, bring consciousness into it.

Spiritual growth isn’t about rejecting life—it’s about bringing the divine into every aspect of life. No one can force another person to grow before they’re ready. If someone thinks success is necessary first, let them follow that path. In time, they will see for themselves what is truly fulfilling. Your role isn’t to convince them otherwise. Your role is simply to stay open, be an example, and hold a space for love and understanding. That is the deepest way to support someone on their journey.

15-1.q: The Surrender Experiment makes it seem like you never say no to what is presented to you. How do you distinguish between saying no because of personal resistance versus rejecting a genuinely bad choice?
15-1.a:
The teachings are not that you should always say yes to everything or avoid asserting will when it’s needed. Surrender is about letting go of your reactive responses and dealing with things from a place of clarity and logic. It is not about doing or not doing—it is about your deepest inner intent.

If you are saying yes because your lower tendencies and habits are driving you to do so, you should try saying no, in order to challenge the power those lower forces have over you. Likewise, if you are saying no because of a stubborn streak that you simply don’t want to rise above, then you should try saying yes, if for no other reason than to free yourself from those shackles. In the end, it isn’t about yes or no; it’s about your willingness to free yourself so that you can act from the highest place within you.

We are here to learn and grow from our experiences in life. The actual outside events and their outcomes are far less important than the transformation they put us through. Once you truly feel that you are willing to go beyond the petty likes and dislikes that the mind makes up, you will begin to make decisions that come from a deeper place. As you willingly let go of the habitual thoughts and emotional patterns that bind you to the limits of your personal self, you will naturally begin to be guided by an overwhelming sense of love and service to life.

15-2.q: When is the voice in my head just a thought, and when is it actually me? If I have to think through a major life decision, isn’t that “me” doing it? If I ignore that voice, how do I make decisions?
15-2.a:
The voice of the mind is never you—you are the one who is aware of the voice. You are the one who is watching the mind try to decide whether to change your career or move abroad or do anything else. Those are thoughts; they are just something you are aware of. Even the uncomfortable feeling that you need to make a decision is not you. You are the one who is aware of all the commotion and anxiety being generated around this decision. Before you can interact properly with life, you must first establish yourself in the seat of Self by letting go of the mind’s noise.

Once established in your seat of consciousness, you will see that nothing your mind ever says is you. Just as your reflection in a mirror is never you—it is simply something you are seeing—so the mind’s thoughts are never you; they are simply something you are seeing. But just because you are not the mind doesn’t mean you cannot use the mind. The mind is meant to be used. The question is, are you using it properly? Most of the thoughts you hear in your mind are personal thoughts—they are about what you want or don’t want. Those thoughts are unnecessary, and your spiritual work is to learn not to listen to those thoughts. Such personal thoughts are just noise interfering with your ability to harmonize with the flow of life.

That doesn’t mean that the analytical mind is not helpful. The mind is brilliant—it is an amazing tool for analyzing and creating. The mind created the computer, the rocket ship, and air conditioning—it is awesome! By all means, use it constructively to create and build and learn.

15-3.q: If we are meant to surrender to life’s unfolding, how do we make decisions? My mind keeps going over and over the possible choices in the situation I’m in. How do I navigate this?
15-3.a:
I cannot help you make a decision one way or another, but I can help you explore the basis of decision-making. Decisions are difficult because we are trying to use them to get what we want and avoid what we don’t want. We are trying to use them to take care of our attachments, desires, and fears. When you are truly letting go of yourself, and have done so for a long time, decisions seem to fade away by themselves—there is just interaction with what is in front of you. That doesn’t mean that you won’t participate in change outside. Everything still happens—it just happens in accordance with God’s laws, instead of your desires. You still have things to do, but you are no longer acting out of the personal motives of need and fear.

A great being interacts in this world out of the sheer joy and love of interacting. If something in front of you can be improved and raised, then you put your whole being into it. You do the best you can at whatever you interact with, just for the joy of the interaction. You are not seeking the fruits of your actions—your actions are simply the expression of the love you feel for everything and everyone around you. You are fine no matter what happens, and you honor and respect whatever is put in front of you. This is the Dharma. The key is: Once you are in a self-sustained state of contentment within, you won’t be trying to use life to make you okay—you are already okay. At this stage, decisions carry no pressure. They carry excitement about what will come next, regardless of what path unfolds.

In the meantime, relax and enjoy making a choice if you need to. Take the pressure off and enjoy your life. Whatever choice you make, put your whole heart and soul into that path. Never look back; never second-guess yourself. Just use the path you have chosen to let go of your personal doubts and fears and be happy to live each day. If you always do this, you will always have made the right decision.

15-4.q: Can you clarify the difference between judgment and discernment? For example, how do I avoid judgment while still using discernment in work or practical situations?
15-4.a:
In order to make rational decisions, of course you use discernment. But discernment is not judgment. Judgment is when you impose your personal preferences, fears, or conditioning onto a situation. It’s when you decide that someone is good or bad, right or wrong, based on your own likes and dislikes. That’s very different from simply seeing what is in front of you and making a rational decision.

There is nothing wrong with rational thinking—it’s a wonderful thing. The problem is when the mind is being used to serve your personal self instead of serving truth. If you fall in love with someone and then find out they are already married, you probably should use discernment. That’s not judgment; that’s clarity. If you are hiring someone for a position and one candidate is more qualified than the other, choosing the right person isn’t judgment—it’s simply making a clear decision based on the reality of the situation.

Judgment happens when you bring your personal self into it. “I don’t like them because they are different from me. I don’t approve of what they do.” That’s personal, and it only happens when you are not okay inside yourself. If you were okay, you wouldn’t need to judge—you would just see. You would respond appropriately to the moment without adding your personal noise to it. That’s the difference.

Learn to observe yourself. Are you making choices based on your personal likes and dislikes, or are you using objective discernment? If there’s resistance, frustration, or a sense of superiority, then you’re in judgment. If there’s clarity, ease, and no inner struggle, then you’re using discernment. Let your decisions flow from reality, not from your personal mind. You will make much better decisions, and you will move through life with more joy and freedom.

15-5.q: I often struggle with making personal decisions and feel paralyzed by the fear of making the wrong choice. How can I overcome this?
15-5.a:
Of course you’re struggling with decisions—how could you not? Look at what you’re asking your mind to do. You want it to tell you which choice will make you happy and which one will make you suffer. Your mind doesn’t know this. It only knows what it has experienced before, and it hasn’t yet experienced the current choice. So the mind starts trying on different scenarios like outfits in a dressing room—spinning them around, analyzing them from every angle—but nothing quite fits. That’s why you feel stuck—you’re asking your mind to do something it simply can’t do.

At its core, most decision-making is simply an attempt to be psychic. You’re trying to predict the future and make sure you won’t regret your choices. With difficult decisions, your mind doesn’t really know which path will lead to happiness. Yet you keep going back to it, expecting it to figure it out. It’s like using a broken calculator and getting frustrated when it won’t give you the right answer. Stop all the struggling and admit the truth: your mind doesn’t know, and that’s okay. Instead of obsessing over which choice is right, recognize that you’re going to be fine either way. Your well-being isn’t determined by these external circumstances—it’s determined by you.

If you want to break free from this paralysis, you need to transform your entire approach. Instead of trying to force a decision, just relax. Let go of the idea that one choice is going to make everything perfect and the other will ruin your life. That’s not how it works. You will be fine either way because you’re going to choose to be fine. Once you stop making it all so heavy, you’ll notice something incredible: a natural flow will emerge. If you stay open, life will start giving you information, little clues about which way to move. You’re not deciding—you’re gathering information. At some point, the decision will simply unfold, without all the mental commotion.

Simply take a step back. Tell your mind it doesn’t have to figure it out. Its job is to relax, be open, and pay attention to what is unfolding. Once you know you will be okay either way, life becomes an exciting adventure instead of a struggle. In the end, life has much more to give you than you could ever take from it.

15-6.q: How does intent influence major life decisions, such as career or relationships?
15-6.a:
Your intent is everything. It’s not about whether you choose one career over another, or whether you enter a relationship or stay single. The real question is: Where are you coming from when you make these decisions? Are you acting from a place of clarity and openness, or are you trying to fix something inside yourself by rearranging the world outside? If your intent is to find happiness through external circumstances—the perfect job, the perfect partner, the perfect path—you’re setting yourself up for suffering. None of those things will ever be exactly what you think they should be.

Instead of looking outward for fulfillment, turn your attention inward. See if your intent is being driven by personal need, by the idea that something outside is going to make you okay inside. If that’s your intent, then you’re using career, relationships, or even spirituality as a means of escape rather than as a way to grow. The key is to stop using life to try to fix yourself. Instead, use life to let go of what’s blocking you from already being okay. That’s a very different approach.

You don’t avoid making choices. You still choose a career, you still enter relationships, but you do it with a different intent. You do it because it’s what’s unfolding in front of you, not because you think it will complete you. When challenges arise, and they will, use them to let go of the parts of you that resist and cling. Imagine if two people entered a relationship not to get something from each other, but as a way to let go of themselves—to support each other in releasing whatever gets in the way of unconditional love. That’s a whole different level of being.

Stop defining yourself by what you do, who you’re with, or what path you take. None of those things are you. You are the one experiencing them. Keep your intent pure—let life unfold, use each moment to grow, and stop thinking anything outside of you is going to solve your inner struggles. When you live that way, your decisions stop being a source of stress. They simply become part of the beautiful unfolding of life.

15-7.q: What made you decide to dedicate your life to helping others?
15-7.a:
In a life of total surrender, you don’t decide to help people. That’s not how it works. You don’t sit there and say, “I want to be a spiritual teacher who helps others.” That’s just the mind trying to create an identity, trying to take ownership of something that isn’t personal. You let go of yourself, and life unfolds in a way that serves the greater whole. If you let go—if you truly surrender— all of this happens by itself.

You don’t have to figure out what you’re supposed to do. You just have to stop interfering. You let go of the noise in your mind: what you want, what you don’t want, who you like, who you don’t like—all of it. You leave space, and something much greater than you moves through that space and serves unconditionally. That’s how you serve. Not by deciding, but by getting out of the way. When you truly surrender, life flows in a way that lifts everything around you.

15-8.q: I am struggling with making a decision to undergo surgery, given its potential risks. How does surrender apply when a person is faced with difficult decisions where there is no clear choice?
15-8.a:
Spiritual surrender is never about not making a decision—it’s about using the situation, as difficult as it may be, to let go of your personal self. The truth is, your personal mind and emotions don’t know what to do, and that’s why you are struggling so much. Surrender starts with accepting that reality: I have an illness, and I don’t know the best way to proceed with treatment. That better be okay with you, because it’s the truth.

Once you are at peace with the fact that there is no clear answer as to the best path forward, you accept that you are not in control of the outcome. No matter what you choose, you might have been better off the other way. You will never know the answer to that, and that is where acceptance becomes essential.

Now comes the really deep part. Once you are at peace with all of this, choose a path forward that is not based on fear. Fear does not make good decisions—cull out any options that are based merely on fear. What may be left are two or more options that seem equally reasonable, given the information you have at the time. Fine—since there is no way of knowing which will yield the best outcome, choose one, and be at peace that you did your absolute best. Let that choice be your solid ground. Never look back or second-guess based on hindsight. Honor the situation, honor your decision, and honor the results.

This is surrender, and it leads to the highest inner states. This is how you use difficult situations to free yourself from yourself. If you are a spiritually oriented person, offer it to God: “I did my best to serve the situation put before me, now I place it all in the hands of reality. I am at peace with the whole thing.” I know this is very deep, and it may seem impossible, but you are in there, and you are higher than all the noise your mind is making.

Now you understand that surrender is something you do inside yourself. It always involves letting go of personal fears and desires in order to live life from a place of absolute clarity and peace.

16-1.q: How can we use the practice of surrender to grow and act with higher leverage in business or professional life?
16-1.a:
The key to using surrender as a tool for growth in business or professional life is to stay conscious and open in the face of what is unfolding in front of you. Life is always presenting you with moments—phone calls, emails, meetings, unexpected demands. The question is, can you meet those moments with clarity and presence instead of resistance, worry, or stress? That is the practice. Instead of getting caught up in anxious thoughts about how much there is to do, stay centered and handle what is right in front of you with a calm, open heart. This is how you turn your professional life into a spiritual path.

Business, especially at higher levels, always involves more work than you can possibly complete. That’s just the nature of it. You will never get it all done, so the real question is, how do you handle that reality? Most people spend their energy stressing about what they aren’t getting done, which drains them and makes them less effective. You can take a different approach. You can stay centered, do the best you can with what’s in front of you, and then let go. The work will always be there, but your inner state doesn’t have to be dictated by it.

A practical way to apply this is to prioritize. When you do what is truly necessary first, you will find that some things simply fall away. If something is important, it will come back to you. If it doesn’t, then it was never that urgent to begin with. Instead of chasing every task with anxiety, you learn to flow with what actually needs your attention. You’re not controlling everything— you’re aligning yourself with what naturally unfolds. That’s a whole different way of engaging with work, and it makes you far more effective than those around you who are lost in stress and overthinking.

Use business as a practice of surrender. Be fully present with each task, but don’t attach yourself to the outcome. Accept what comes, do what you can, and let go of what you can’t. In doing this, you will not only excel in your work, but you will also grow spiritually. That growth will set you apart—not because you’re forcing success, but because you’re operating from a place of clarity, balance, and trust. That’s the highest leverage you can have.

16-2.q: I run a successful business. How do I approach business decisions while remaining aligned with the practice of surrender?
16-2.a:
Amazingly, the answer you seek is the essence of the teaching in the Bhagavad Gita. Though it is considered a holy book—some say even the Hindu Bible— its teachings are very practical in regard to the highest way to interact with life. In a nutshell, it says do the absolute best at whatever you are doing, but don’t do it for personal gain—do it as an act of service to the Universe. You don’t surrender doing your best; you surrender the personal motives for doing or not doing what is put before you.

You are a businessperson running a business the Universe has given to you. You do business just as any other excellent businessperson would do it. But you renounce the fruits of your actions. You are not doing it for you—you are doing it as an expression of perfection. Make good business decisions— not out of fear or greed, but out of rational, clear judgement based on what’s best for the business. Make believe God came down and gave you this business to run for Him. It’s not yours—you are running it for Him. Now, do your best to run it to the best of your ability—fearlessly and selflessly.

16-3.q: I have spent years exploring goal and intention setting, but it seems more natural to surrender to life’s flow. Does goal setting have a place in spiritual practice?
16-3.a:
There is nothing wrong with intention or goal setting. The question is, on what basis are you setting those intentions and goals? If you’re setting your intentions based on needs, fears, or desires, then the best that will happen is that needs, fears, and desires will be guiding your life. From a spiritual point of view, no meaningful success can come from that.

A spiritual person works at a much deeper level than fears and desires. If you set your life’s aspirations on the highest aspects of yourself, you’ll quickly notice that fears and desires are what keep you from your God-realized state. It will become obvious that you must relax through the powerful draw of these very human, psychological aspects of your being. This cannot be done in one fell swoop. You have to learn how to let go of the pull of the personal on a moment-to-moment, day-by-day basis. Start from where you are by honestly recognizing the root cause of your fears and desires. You’re still in your daily life, but instead of putting your will into getting or avoiding, you put your will into constantly relaxing and releasing.

Amazingly, as you let go of yourself, you will know what you are supposed to be doing. Your life becomes a moment-to-moment service to the unfolding of life. The personal falls off, and what is left is what we call the Dharma—that which you would be doing if you had no personal motive but were simply here to serve God. This is called “The Pathless Path,” and it stretches from where you are now to the perfection of your merger with God.

16-4.q: What is the difference between striving for excellence and being trapped in perfectionism? I am struggling with the balance between accepting life as it unfolds and doing my best to serve it.
16-4.a:
Surrender is not about being passive or lazy. The flow of life will always give you work and service to do, and by all means, do the best you can with all your tasks in life. The difference between doing your best and being a perfectionist all comes down to your root intent. If you are striving to do your best out of love for expressing yourself and giving your best to life as an act of service and beauty, this is a great spiritual practice. If you are striving to do the best you can because you are neurotic about making everything perfect and are driven by perfectionism out of fear of failure or disapproval, then your intent is coming from a place of disturbance. Striving for excellence comes from enthusiasm, love, and inspiration and has nothing to do with others, except the Creator of the Universe, who gave you the ability to serve with all your heart.

If you feel the act of doing your best is coming from a place of disturbance, then work on letting go of those fears while you still strive to do your very best. The key is to let go of the personal, do your very best, then be happy with whatever comes back. The outcome of the best that you can do is a very beautiful and honorable thing, regardless of how the outside world judges it.

16-5.q: I am passionate about building my business and also very committed to my spiritual growth. How do the concepts of surrender and non-doership work together with building a successful outer life?
16-5.a:
The short answer is that the cleaner you are inside, the more natural your outer life will be. It all comes down to motive—why are you making plans and striving outside? If you are not okay inside and are striving externally to try to be okay, that is a very difficult life: trying to fix the inside with the outside. If, on the other hand, you are wonderful inside—filled with energy, love, and inspiration—and you are expressing that outside, that is a totally different story. Expressing your inner beauty outside can certainly involve planning and putting your whole being into your work. First, fix the inside so that you are whole and complete within yourself, then do your absolute best to express your inner greatness in the world—if for no other reason than love wants to give and inspiration wants to create.

This is what it means “to be in the world but not of it.” The fact is, you live inside, and once you cleanse the inside of all the blockages you have accumulated, your energy will be free to flow abundantly. Life will then naturally give you service to do—that is what is meant by the Tao and your Dharma. There are no desires or personal motives. You are a whole being in harmony with the flow of life. Once you do the inner work to transcend the personal, there is no conflict between completely surrendering inside and doing your absolute best to serve outside.

16-6.q: How do I balance a hectic, demanding life with the need for inner peace and devotion? Do I need to find the time to slow down, turn inward, and overcome stress and energy blockages with spiritual practices?
16-6.a:
Stress is not due to how busy you are. Stress is due to how much resistance you are asserting while you are doing what you are doing. Work is not stress; it is service to the universe. God has given you a task to do while you spin around dark, empty space. It has no real meaning except as an act of service. We are all going to die soon, and we are not going to take anything of this world with us. Stress is caused by ego thinking there is something to get and something to lose. We constantly feel that whatever we are doing is not enough. There are always other things we must be doing to succeed and not fail.

The secret to life is to do your best at whatever you are doing in the moment, and then serve what comes next. Renounce the fruits of your actions and let the joy of service be your sole intent—every moment. Working, taking care of family, taking care of others—all of it is a gift you are giving to God. That is how to feel close to God in the midst of daily life. Offer everything you do as an act of devotion to God.

If you are taking on too many tasks and getting overwhelmed, ask yourself why you are doing that. Is it fear of failure? Is it to gain acceptance and not feel rejected or criticized? Those are all ego issues. Don’t serve your ego; serve God. There is a natural balance, but you will never find it until you devote yourself to the Universal Flow instead of your ego. Read Living Untethered and start with the small stuff you are bothering yourself about. An important quote from that book is, “The moment in front of you is not bothering you. You are bothering yourself about the moment in front of you.” Stop doing that, and the stress will melt away. Meditation and time in quietude are also very helpful. Do what you can, but don’t make it just another source of stress. Let it be another act of service.

16-7.q: How do I approach my sales job and caregiving for my father without becoming overwhelmed or feeling unsuccessful?
16-7.a:
Your job and your caregiving are not separate from your spiritual path—they are your spiritual path. The idea that spiritual practice only happens when you meditate or listen to talks, and then you have to go back to your “real life,” is an illusion. Life itself is your practice. Your sales calls, your father’s illness, your frustrations, your disappointments—these are all opportunities for growth. The real work is not about changing those external situations; it’s about letting go of the part of you that resists them. That’s where the suffering comes from—not from what’s happening, but from your reaction to it.

Start to watch yourself. You’ll see how certain things make you uncomfortable—maybe a rejection on the phone; maybe something difficult with your father. Notice how the mind starts creating resistance: I don’t like this. I wish this wasn’t happening. This is hard. This isn’t fair. That’s what is causing the disturbance, not the situation itself. Your job isn’t to fix the outside world so that it matches what you want—it’s to let go of the part of you that insists on things being a certain way. Whenever you notice tension and resistance, just relax, breathe, and let it go. You won’t be perfect at it, and that’s okay. Just keep practicing.

As you do this, something remarkable starts to happen. The very things that used to bother you don’t disturb you anymore. The caregiving, the sales calls, the challenges—they don’t change; you do. Because you’re not wasting your energy resisting, you’re actually performing better. If you’re relaxed and open, you’re naturally more effective. If you fight everything, you’re tight, you’re reactive, and you suffer.

This is your spiritual work. You’re not escaping your responsibilities but using them as a means to let go of yourself. That’s freedom. That’s peace.

The very same life that once overwhelmed you can become your doorway to liberation.

16-8.q: I struggle with colleagues who are driven by ego, fear, and greed. How do I interact with negative people in my work environment while staying true to spiritual principles?
16-8.a:
The key is to always let go of your personal reactions first. If you find that you feel resistance to someone whose behavior is coming from a place of ego, let go of the part of you that is not able to handle that. You will find in many cases that the highest thing you can do with someone’s negative behavior is to let go of your resistance. The very fact that you aren’t pushing their negative energy back at them can transform the relationship.

Of course, there are times when a situation calls for action. In those cases, first let go of your personal reactions and preferences, then act from the highest clarity available to bring about the best possible outcome. I know it is hard to believe at first, but if you drop your resistance, you can actually take the attitude of serving the people around you—even if they are not so spiritual. That is good for you and good for them.

16-9.q: I’m a business owner and challenged with managing negativity among employees. What is the balance between stepping in and taking control of the situation versus allowing life the time to naturally work it out?
16-9.a:
Surrender is about letting go of your reactive response and then dealing with things from a place of clarity and logic. It is all about your intent. If you are letting go sincerely, and circumstances are such that you need to take action for the good of the employees and your company, first let go of your reactive energies, then act from a place of clarity.

Let your actions come from sincerely seeking the best overall solution to the situation. Be sure to listen to the issues your employees are having, and then work consciously to bring about the highest outcome possible for all parties.

That said, there will be times that you simply have to let an employee go because of the disruptive energy they insist on creating. You are the boss, and it is your responsibility to create a productive work environment for your employees. But don’t do it because you can’t handle the situation. Do it because you can handle the situation, and this is the best way to move forward.

16-10.q: Is it helpful for my growth to have other goals besides spiritual realization?
16-10.a:
The answer is yes—because the highest realization naturally includes engaging with life. It’s not about isolating yourself on some mountaintop or cutting yourself off from the world. It’s about bringing higher energy into everything you do. You don’t have to become a priest, a monk, or some spiritual recluse. You can live in the world. You can have relationships. You can run a business. The real question isn’t whether you should have goals—it’s whether your goals are rooted in truth. A spiritual life doesn’t mean rejecting external goals; it means living in a way that raises everything around you.

That’s the highest life you can live. Every moment that unfolds before you is an opportunity to uplift the energy of that moment. When someone yells at you, you don’t yell back. You quietly see if there is something you can say or do to uplift the energy being expressed. You walk through life leaving everything better than you found it—not by forcing or controlling, but simply by being in harmony with what is.

The drive for success often stems from a desire to fill an inner void or seek meaning for your life. Spiritual growth encourages addressing these inner needs directly, rather than relying on external achievements for fulfillment. By letting go of attachments to outcomes, you can engage in pursuits with clarity and purpose, making success a byproduct of authentic action rather than an ego-driven goal. This balance allows you to enjoy the process of life while staying aligned with your spiritual values.

So yes, you set goals, but not in the way the world teaches you. Not as a way to get something from life, but as a way to give yourself fully to it. Whether you’re leading a company, raising a family, or just walking down the street, you bring that deeper awareness into every action. That’s the goal— because in the end, there’s no separation between spiritual realization and life itself. They are one and the same.

17-1.q: Are relationships meant to teach us about overcoming ourselves?
17-1.a:
Relationships are about growth. You think you’re looking for someone who aligns with you perfectly, but what you’re really doing is looking for someone who won’t challenge your preferences, your past experiences, or your expectations. That’s not love. That’s you trying to hold on to yourself. The truth is, relationships are one of the greatest opportunities for spiritual growth. This is because they expose the places inside of you where you are still holding on and needing things to be a certain way in order to feel okay.

When you enter a relationship, you open. Your heart opens, your expectations open, and suddenly, things are flowing. But the moment something happens that doesn’t match what you want, you start to close. You think, Maybe this isn’t the right person. Maybe I made a mistake. What if the whole point of the relationship isn’t getting what you want? What if it’s about learning how to stay open, how to let go of yourself, and how to love beyond your personal conditions?

If you were given a relationship where nothing ever challenged you, you would never grow. You would never be pushed beyond your own limitations. That’s why there is no such thing as a perfect match—because the world isn’t supposed to give you a person who fits all your preferences like a checklist. It’s supposed to give you a person who helps you see the parts of yourself that you are still clinging to and having trouble letting go of. If you’re willing to use your relationships for your spiritual growth, then any relationship you are committed to can become meaningful.

So don’t keep trying to find the one person who won’t challenge you. Instead, find the part of you that wants to be challenged, that wants to grow, that wants to love beyond your own limitations. That’s what relationships are really for—not to reinforce who you think you are, but to help you transcend into who you really are.

17-2.q: I have successfully applied the teachings to my family relationships, but I
17-2.a:
still feel blocked in my relationship with my spouse. Is it really possible to let go of my blockages in this area?

You obviously have been trying to apply the teachings to your life, and relationships are where many people stumble. In truth, relationships are very simple—we make them complicated. If you are not okay inside and you are expecting a relationship to make you okay, you are already off to a bad start. Another human being cannot make you okay—all they can do is distract you from yourself or attempt to compensate for your inner issues. That type of relationship does not work and can never last at a healthy level—especially for someone who is trying to grow spiritually.

In contrast, a healthy relationship starts with the relationship with yourself. If you are giving yourself a hard time in there, how can you expect that someone outside of you is going to make it all okay? First, you have to learn to get along with yourself. You have to learn to let go of the blockages that are holding you back from the highest expression of yourself. This is your work, not someone else’s. Once you are committed to working on yourself and not expecting someone else to make things okay, you can have a healthy, lasting relationship with someone else.

The key to a deep spiritual relationship is there are no expectations that the other person is supposed to be making you okay. That is your job 24/7. The other person is someone you are honored to get to know. There are eight billion people on the planet Earth—you can’t get to know all of them. But you can get to know one special person really well. Great! Enjoy getting to know someone who is nothing like you. Their genetics differ from yours; their formative years were very different from yours; their blockages are different from yours—everything is different from you. Good—enjoy the differences. Do not expect the other person to satisfy your needs and protect you from your fears. You should be letting go of your psychological needs and releasing the causes of your psychological fears. Work to bring your highest self into the relationship. Don’t think that because this is your significant other, they have to handle your blocked energies. Those blocked energies are your work, not theirs.

If you approach your relationships like this, they will be totally supportive of your highest spiritual growth. Do your inner work, and strive to bring into your relationships the most beautiful, open person you can be. If it’s hard to do that, good—that is the spiritual work of letting go of yourself. Bring beauty into this world, and don’t expect anything in return—especially from those who are closest to you. Once you have let go of the blockages holding you back, you will start to feel a flow of joy, love, and inspiration rising up within you. This is your natural, unblocked state. By all means, share that unconditional love with all, especially the people closest to you. This love will never subside, as long as you keep letting go of yourself.

17-3.q: How do I manage relationships while growing spiritually, especially when others don’t understand my changes?
17-3.a:
If you are growing spiritually and the people around you don’t understand, that’s okay. You don’t have to make them understand. Your job is not to explain yourself or to convince anyone to see things your way. Your job is to stay true to your highest intent. If your growth is real, the relationships in your life will shift naturally—some will fall away, and others will deepen. That’s just how life unfolds. You don’t have to force anything, and you don’t have to resist anything. Let things move as they need to move.

Relationships are one of the greatest tools for spiritual growth. If you’re in one, it’s because there’s something there for you to work through. It will bring up your attachments, your fears, your expectations—it will show you all the places where you’re still holding on. That’s a gift. Use it. Let the relationship help you see yourself more clearly. But don’t expect the other person to be on the same journey at the same pace. They are where they are, just as you are where you are. When you truly wake up, you don’t become more demanding in your relationships—you become more willing to serve. You stop needing the other person to be a certain way, and instead, you live to give.

Commitment is powerful. If you’re in a relationship and you’ve committed to it, then use it as part of your path. Commitment means you don’t just walk away because something is difficult, and you don’t let your changing spiritual experiences become a reason to push people away. You stay present, and you learn from what arises. Love isn’t about taking—it’s about giving. If your spiritual growth is real, it will open your heart, not close it. You won’t withdraw from people because they don’t understand you—you’ll just love them anyway. You won’t need anything from them, so you’ll be free to give them everything.

The key is to let go of yourself. Let go of your need to be understood and your need for others to validate your path. Let life unfold naturally. Some relationships will shift, and that’s okay. The ones that are meant to stay will stay. The ones that are meant to change will change. If you stay centered in your highest intent, everything will take care of itself. Keep letting go. Keep surrendering. That’s all you ever have to do.

17-4.q: Is it possible to heal together in a relationship?
17-4.a:
If you are in a relationship and looking to heal together, of course you can. A relationship should not be about making the other person conform to what you think you need. It’s not about controlling each other to avoid getting hurt. Instead, it’s an opportunity to grow together, to use each other as mirrors, and to support each other in letting go of what keeps you from being fully open. You both have your own inner stuff—the key is to recognize that and choose to love each other while the cleansing process takes place.

The way to do this is to give each other the respect and space needed to go through your changes. Commit to letting go of your own inner disturbances to the best of your ability. In doing so, you create an environment where the other person can do the same. It’s not about being perfect. If you fall short, give yourself grace, and give that same grace to your partner as well. That’s how you support each other. If both of you are willing to do this, the relationship becomes a sacred place for growth, rather than a battlefield of personal blockages clashing against each other.

There is an even deeper aspect to this—if you truly learn how to perfect your relationship with one person, it won’t stop there. It will expand into every aspect of your life. The way you interact with your partner will begin to affect the way you interact with the world. When you practice this kind of love and openness in your relationship, it will naturally extend to coworkers, friends, and even strangers. If someone at work has a bad day and takes it out on you, you will have developed the inner strength to not take it personally. You won’t need to react—you’ll simply remain open.

That is what it means to truly heal in a relationship. You don’t just heal each other; you use the relationship to grow into the kind of person who brings love and openness into every part of life. Eventually, your presence itself becomes a gift, not just to your partner, but to the whole world. That’s the real purpose of a relationship—to become more of who you truly are, beyond all the fears and insecurities, until all that’s left is love.

17-5.q: I struggle with knowing when to leave a relationship. If my suffering comes from my ego’s preferences, should I stay to grow? How do I know when a relationship is truly unhealthy and not worth continuing?
17-5.a:
Of course, we cannot give relationship advice—people need to find their own way through these things. But recognize that the real issue is not the decision of whether to leave; it is the motive behind the decision. Life will unfold, and you have a responsibility to use it for your spiritual growth. Get clear, let go of your personal motives, and serve the unfolding of life to the best of your ability.

Relationships last when they have deep growth left; they sometimes end when they are holding one or more of the people back. There is nothing wrong with staying, and there is nothing wrong with leaving. The question is: What is the underlying motive? If your motive is to grow spiritually, and the relationship is not creating growth opportunities, that’s one thing. If you are simply not open inside and want to look for someone who can better satisfy your personal needs, that’s another thing. Be brutally honest with yourself— then make a decision. Make it be the right decision by willfully letting go of the inner turmoil that either decision is going to create.

17-6.q: I’m in a difficult relationship that I’d like to try to salvage. We tend to close when we’re around each other. What can I do to change that dynamic?
17-6.a:
We can certainly choose to use our relationships for our inner growth. Based on the honesty you showed in questioning your role in the relationship, you are very capable of doing that. You can make it a game, like a video game. Can you stay centered during the time you are interacting with your partner? If not, try to see why. Is it that the well has been poisoned by past difficult interactions, and now you close the moment you have to interact? If so, practice staying open deep inside while you let go of whatever comes up in your mind and your emotions. Don’t make the interaction be about your partner—let it be about you and what you see coming up inside. Be polite and pay attention to what is happening outside, but keep an honest eye on what you are experiencing inside.

This is really a great situation for spiritual growth. As you manage to remain clear and nonreactive during the time you spend together, you will get to see if any of this is just you carrying forward hurt and disappointment from the past. Each time you’re together, make believe you have just met—they are a new person every time you interact with them. It can be so much fun and exciting to challenge yourself in this way, and it can completely change the dynamic of the relationship. Just let your intent be to always use the situation to get closer to God, and you can’t go wrong.

17-7.q: How does someone know whether they should leave an abusive relationship?
17-7.a:
There are many types of abuse: physical, emotional, and mental. There is no excuse for physical abuse. If a person stays in a physically abusive relationship, they need to examine why they are staying. A clear person understands that their body is a gift from creation, and they have a responsibility to take care of it and treat it with great respect. There may be fears and needs that keep a person compelled to stay in a physically abusive relationship; they need to work on doing their best to rise above these fears and needs so they can move into a healthier environment.

If the abuse is mental or emotional, it’s a little subtler. If a person has a closed mind, and that mind considers it abusive if they don’t get what they want, that person should use the relationship to be more open and receptive to other people’s views. Not getting what you want is not abusive, per se; we need to be able to handle letting go of our mental preferences. However, if a person’s partner is purposely going out their way to be mentally or emotionally abusive, that is not a healthy environment and has to be dealt with. In this situation, one should stay calm as much as possible so that clear decisions can be made.

17-8.q: How can I teach spiritual resilience to a young child who has experienced hardship?
17-8.a:
The first thing you need to understand about teaching a child resilience is that you don’t teach it through words or structured lessons. You don’t sit them down and explain resilience to them. You live it. You embody it. Children watch you, whether you realize it or not. Over time, they absorb what they see in you. If hardship comes into your life—if you face loss, betrayal, or pain— how do you handle it? Do you break down and fall into judgment and anger, or do you move through it with grace, without closing your heart? That’s what your children will learn from you.

This isn’t about putting on a performance for them. That’s not real enough, and children see through that. You’re not doing it to set an example— you’re doing it because it’s the highest way to live. If you love, even when you are not loved in return, they will see that. If you don’t judge, even when others judge you, they will see that, too. One day, when life presents them with their own challenges, they will find something inside themselves that they didn’t even know was there. It will be a way of being that they absorbed just by growing up around you.

You don’t always know what someone else is getting from you in the moment. Sometimes they don’t even know. But years later, they look back, and something clicks. They remember how you handled things, and in a moment of struggle, they instinctively do the same. Maybe they’re in a difficult relationship, and they recall how you treated them with patience and kindness when they were being difficult. Maybe they face loss, and something in them remembers the way you walked through your own pain with dignity and openness, without shutting down. That’s how they learn. That’s how you give them a very special gift. Give them the gift of having experienced how beautiful a human being can be.

17-9.q: I have a two-year-old daughter. How can I guide her to live with the clarity and freedom I’m now learning to cultivate?
17-9.a:
Your daughter’s first and most powerful teacher is you—not through words or lessons, but through how you are. From the moment she was born, she has been absorbing everything from you—your energy, your emotions, your state of being. She doesn’t just listen to what you say; she feels who you are. So, the greatest gift you can give her is not intellectual teachings, but your own clarity, openness, and presence. If you live in a state of love, peace, and acceptance, she will naturally learn to do the same. If you live with frustration, impatience, or anger, she will learn that too. Your responsibility isn’t to shape her into something—it’s to purify yourself so that she is naturally surrounded by the highest vibration of being.

At two years old, she is not ready for teachings about the mind, about the Self, or about spiritual practice. But she is ready for presence. She is ready to live in an environment where love flows naturally, where she is safe in the presence of someone who is not caught up in their own struggles. The best thing you can do as a parent is to step aside—to get out of the way. Let go of your personal reactions and mental noise. When you do that, something much greater than you can come through. What comes through is pure love and compassionate understanding. That is what raises a child. Not your words, discipline or even your conscious efforts, but the energy that flows in your presence.

Take responsibility for yourself. If you are clear, open, and filled with love, that is what your daughter will know. The world will bring her challenges, no doubt. When she has been raised in clarity, she will meet those challenges with clarity. When she has been raised in love, she will move through life with love. She will not have to learn how to handle difficulties— she will simply handle them because she will not be burdened by the same inner noise that keeps most people trapped.

Let your daughter be your inspiration to do this work. If you want to bring something beautiful to her, commit fully to your own surrender. Let go of yourself before you walk through the door of your home. Before you see her, clear yourself. Do not bring your stress, frustrations, or worries into her world. Make it your practice to be a vessel of love in her presence. That is how you become a great parent—by showing her, through the purity of your being, what it is like to live in the presence of a great human being.

This is not just about parenting. It is about all of life. If you want to bring beauty into your daughter’s life, bring beauty into everything you do. Bring it into your work, your relationships, and the way you walk through the world. Let go of your own baggage so that you can be a force of clarity and love wherever you are. When you do this, you will not only raise your daughter in light—you will walk through life as a beacon of light itself.

17-10.q: How do I handle challenges in relationships with my children?
17-10.a:
The first thing you must understand is that they are not your children in the sense that your mind thinks. They came through you, but they are their own beings, with their own bodies, their own consciousnesses, their own journeys. If you start with the belief that they belong to you, and that their lives must unfold according to your desires, you will struggle. Instead, step back and recognize that they are souls, just like you, navigating this human experience in their own way.

The real challenge is not your children—it is your inability to handle what they bring up in you. When you say, “I can’t handle my kids,” what you’re really saying is, “I can’t handle the experiences that come with being a parent.” Life is full of experiences, and if you can’t handle them, you don’t just suffer—you become part of the problem. Think about it: if you showed up at a car accident and couldn’t handle the sight of blood, you would be of no use to anyone. The same is true in parenting. If you can’t handle the terrible twos, the teenage years, the heartbreaks, the uncertainties, then not only are you not helping your children, but you are adding unnecessary tension to the entire situation.

Where do you start if you’re having trouble with your children? You start with you. Your job isn’t to control your children’s lives or to make everything go the way you want. Your job is to work on yourself so you can handle whatever comes. If you can handle things, you can be supportive and be a source of strength for your family. But if you’re always caught up in your own fears and anxieties about your children, you are not helping them; you are just adding noise to the situation. Instead, commit to handling life. Say to yourself, I can handle this. Whatever stage my children are in, whatever they go through, I can handle it.

Ultimately, the highest truth is that you are not in control. If you can step aside, if you can let go of the neurotic part of you that tries to control everything, then something much higher will flow through you. The real parent is not your small self—it is something divine. And when you get out of the way, that higher force can take care of things in a way your mind cannot. This is how you truly serve as a parent—not by worrying, not by controlling, but by making space for something greater to flow through you.

The next time you feel overwhelmed—stop, breathe, and remind yourself, I can handle this. Let go of the mental noise and allow yourself to be a conduit for something higher. That is how you truly help your children—not by gripping tighter, but by bringing clarity into situations as they unfold.

18-1.q: In The Surrender Experiment, you wrote about letting go of personal preferences and allowing life to unfold. If you do this, how will you know when you really do need to act?
18-1.a:
If you want to grow spiritually, the first thing to do is let go of your personal reaction to what life is presenting you. But that’s not the end of it. Life is not passive; it’s interactive. Once you have let go of your personal self by relaxing through the noise of likes and dislikes, you are left to deal directly with reality, instead of your habit-formed reactions to it. You will know what to do. It is not so complicated, once like and dislike are out of the picture.

For example, if someone is suing you for something you didn’t do, you have an obligation to defend yourself. Clearly, there are situations that require action. The key is to remain centered, not reactive, while doing so. If you can do this, you will find a quiet guidance from within that is easily missed when your mind and your heart are screaming about how you want things to be.

That is an act of inner surrender. First let go of the personal, then see what life is doing and interact appropriately and intelligently. In time, all your interactions with life will seem like acts of service, and they will all be done with a sense of great love. You become a servant of the present moment, and your only goal is to make sure that every moment that passes before you is better off because it did.

18-2.q: You often talk about letting go of the small stuff, the low-hanging fruit. But what about the more disturbing events in life, like violence, racism, pollution, or severe illness? How can we let go when terrible things are happening in this world?
18-2.a:
We understand your desire to address how to let go when it comes to the bigger things in life. The key is that if you aren’t practicing regularly with the small things, it will be much more difficult to release the bigger ones, because you haven’t learned how to handle your inner resistance. Don’t worry about the big stuff right now. Instead, practice every day with every situation that causes inner resistance. The earlier you catch your tendency to resist, and then relax and let go, the easier the process will be.

With that said, you need to understand that when it comes to disharmony in life, there is a spiritual aspect to these things also. You begin by deeply accepting that even these difficult things are part of reality. If you cannot accept this truth, you will become disturbed and incapable of dealing with situations in a productive way. A disturbed person is so absorbed in their inner disturbance that their entire motivation becomes finding a way to end it. They are not really dealing with the outside situation that triggered the disturbance; they are dealing with the inner disturbance itself.

A deep being begins by accepting reality. If something has happened, then it has happened. You cannot undo what has already happened. Acceptance doesn’t mean you enjoy what happened; it simply means you can handle the fact that it took place. Find the place of peace within you that does not judge reality but strives to serve it. Ultimately, you learn to honor, respect, and love reality so much that you live and breathe to serve every moment that unfolds before you. If harmony unfolds before you, rejoice in it. If disharmony unfolds before you, consciously work to raise it as it passes by.

All of this is done with a sense of love and honor.

In the end, if you act from a place of disturbance, you are bringing disturbance into this world. If you act from a place of peace, love, and respect, then you are bringing peace, love, and respect into this world. An evolved being is not here to be disturbed by this world—they are here to serve it.

18-3.q: How can I embody nonviolence (ahimsa) in daily life?
18-3.a:
Ahimsa—nonviolence—is not just about how you act in the external world; it is also about how you treat everything that comes up inside of you. It is an absolute commitment to not create violence, and that includes how you interact with your own mind and emotions. If difficult thoughts or feelings come up, you don’t push them away. That would be a form of inner violence. Instead, you love them. You allow them to come up, you honor them for the role they played in your growth, and you release them with gratitude.

Loving what comes up inside you is a form of letting go. You are not struggling against your own thoughts, resisting your past, or condemning yourself for what you’ve been through. When you can love your past fully, it loses its power over you—it dissolves. When you embrace everything inside you, the struggle ends. The Bhagavad Gita says: raise the self with Self; do not trample down the self. That means your work is not to suppress or reject what arises within you, but to uplift it and transform it through love.

This extends beyond just your current situation. Everything that has ever happened to you, even the most difficult experiences, has played a role in shaping who you are. If you look back and see only resentment or regret, that is violence toward yourself. Instead, see that every experience, good or bad, has helped you evolve. The people who hurt you, the relationships that didn’t work out, the hardships that tested you—they all gave you something. They made you stronger, wiser, more capable of handling life. Instead of carrying your past as a weight, honor it, love it, and be sure to thank it.

When you live this way, you embody nonviolence at the deepest level. It’s not only about not harming others—it’s about not harming yourself. It’s about meeting life, inside and out, with total openness. No resistance, no suppression, no struggle. Just a deep, abiding love for whatever comes up, knowing that it is all part of your journey home.

18-4.q: How can I contribute positively to a chaotic world without being overwhelmed by frustration?
18-4.a:
If you find yourself overwhelmed by frustration with the state of the world, you must first recognize reality as it is. There will always be people cutting down trees for profit, leaders waging wars for power, and individuals making choices that seem destructive or ignorant. That is the nature of the world. The real question is not whether these things happen—it’s whether you are going to let them disturb your inner state so that you become ineffective, lost in anger, or consumed by despair. If you cannot handle what is happening around you, you cannot help.

Begin by handling it. That means stepping back and realizing that reality is unfolding as it always has, with both beauty and destruction. Your role is not to fight reality with resistance, but to bring something higher into it. You don’t have to agree with what’s happening, and you don’t have to disengage either. What you must do is find a place inside yourself where you can witness the chaos of the world without being thrown off-center. If you allow frustration, hatred, or despair to take hold and overwhelm you, then you are no longer contributing—you are just another person lost in reactivity.

Once you have established that inner steadiness, then you act. You do what you can to help, not because you’re upset but because you have something to offer. If that means standing in front of a tree to protect it, do it. If that means working toward solutions in a peaceful, constructive way, do it. But don’t do it because you can’t handle what is happening; do it because you are strong enough to bring clarity and love into a situation that desperately needs it.

This world does not need more people who are lost in disturbance. It needs people who can stand in the middle of it all and bring light. Let that be your practice. Start with handling the inner disturbance, then bring your best self forward. This is how you contribute to a chaotic world without being overwhelmed by it.

18-5.q: How do we deal with evil in the world, such as people who harm innocent people?
18-5.a:
People have asked many times about the injustices and evils in this world. Interestingly, we don’t generally call animals evil when they hurt each other; we understand they are just following their lower instincts. But humans are capable of rising above their lower instincts—if they choose to do so. More importantly, humans have a much more complex psychological aspect of their being—their advanced thoughts and emotions.

When that psychological aspect becomes blocked by suppressed past experiences, many people try to release the blocked energy by acting out externally. This release can be very damaging to those around them. When a person becomes disturbed enough inside, they can become so dark and warped that the only way for them to find release is to harm others. Sometimes they are motivated by some perceived personal gain—but sometimes there is no perceived gain except the release of the darkness that has manifested inside. We view a person who brings such extreme darkness into this world as evil.

Evil is a terrible thing, but it is part of reality. If a river becomes blocked, it floods innocent people who live upstream. If a person becomes blocked, they can hurt innocent people who live around them. The only solution is for people to be taught how to process the difficulties of life instead of suppressing them. That is part of the evolution of humanity. In the meantime, we cannot let other people’s disturbances cause us to become blocked. We have to be able to process reality, and then do what we can to raise the world as it passes before us.

18-6.q: I was in an abusive relationship, and I struggle daily with deep emotional pain and shame. What advice do you have for truly healing?
18-6.a:
The experience you struggle with is undoubtedly painful. To begin truly healing, it is important to understand that the process of letting go is the same whether you are letting go of the small stuff or the big stuff, like this. The problem is that if you’re not practicing regularly with the small stuff, it will be much more difficult to let go with the big stuff. This is because you haven’t learned how to handle your inner resistance. Start the healing process by practicing every day with all the small situations that cause inner resistance. The earlier you catch your resistance and let go, the easier the process will be. In addition, the energy of fear that is so closely tied to deep emotional pain, such as trauma, tends to show up throughout the day in simple, smaller fears and resistances. If you focus on letting go when these daily fears come up, you will find that, over time, even deep emotional pain can gradually diminish.

Obviously, events can be traumatic and very difficult to deal with when they take place. The key to a beautiful, healthy life is to let go of these painful impressions as soon as possible. The problem is we try to adjust our lives so we don’t have to deal with the continuing sense of discomfort. Instead, we need to learn to let go of the root blockages, the samskaras, that are causing the continuing sense of discomfort.

It is important to change your attitude and be positive about the possibility of living your life free from stored pain. You don’t have to fight the samskaras; you simply have to relax and release to the best of your ability when they begin to surface. Eventually, you will have worked through your past blockages, and you will get to deal with the joy of having freed yourself.

18-7.q: I was sexually assaulted many years ago and have been through therapy, but I still struggle with trauma. I have read your books and practiced letting go, but this pain seems impossible to release. How can I finally free myself from it?
18-7.a:
It hurts my heart just reading what you went through. I am so sorry that you had to endure that terrible experience. But you weren’t seeking my sympathy; you were asking how to let the stored pain go. That is a very deep request. Many people, for reasons that are entirely understandable, don’t really want to hear the deep answer. But you asked, and from a spiritual point of view, here is the answer:

1.	You must really want to let it go, no matter what it takes. This means you are willing to go through the pain of letting it go.

That must be your honest intent throughout the process.

2.	Accept that the event happened. This has nothing to do with right or wrong—it has to do with reality. And the reality is that no matter what you do, you will never be able to make the event not have happened. As terrible as it was, it did happen. And you must be ready to accept that it was part of your life experiences while visiting the planet Earth.

3.	This is the hardest part—you must try to stop feeling sorry that it happened. Feeling sorry for yourself does not help. You are a great being who had a terrible experience. It does not define you, though right now it may feel as though it does. The experience came and it went like all of life’s experiences. If you really want it to stop haunting you, you must be willing to forgive and to release the samskara it left, so you can move on.

4.	If you really want your mind and your heart to be cleansed of this, use affirmation. Acknowledge that what you went through was a life experience that can help you grow and make you stronger. As long as you harbor fear and pain about the experience, you will continue suppressing it and keeping it buried inside. Better to be bold—embrace the challenge of letting go. Whatever you do, don’t keep it in there ruining your life.

5.	When the event comes back up in your mind or heart—welcome it. Tell it that it is free to come up, and now it is free to release. To truly release it, your heart and mind must be open so that the energy can finally finish its journey through you without your resistance. This will take time, but you can do this if you’re really ready to let the past event go. Each time it shows its head, give it a kiss, like you would a child that went through a bad experience. Hug it, tell it everything is okay now, and it is free to come up and continue its journey through the universe of time and space. You must be positive about this process of letting go. Love the process—be excited to let go.

6.	It takes a great being to do this, but you don’t have to do it alone. You can offer the disturbed energy up to God (if that is your path) or release it into the vast universe of outer space. Just don’t own it anymore—give it away. It’s a bad memory that got stuck inside. It cannot harm you—that part was over long ago. Love the process of letting go.

7.	When you are able to smile again, from the depth of your being, you will be done with the entire event. And those around you will be able to feel the difference. This is the greatest gift you can give to your family and friends, and to yourself, for the rest of your life. In truth, it is a gift to all of humanity. Christ turned water into wine—you turned darkness into light.

19-1.q: How do I open my heart and keep it open?
19-1.a:
If you want to open your heart, don’t focus on trying to force it open—focus on why it’s closed in the first place. Your heart is naturally open. It is your default state. But over time you’ve built walls around it, trying to protect yourself from pain, disappointment, or fear. The real work is not in opening your heart, but in letting go of the things that make you close it.

You close your heart because you are trying to protect yourself. Maybe you’ve been hurt; maybe you’re afraid of rejection; maybe you have expectations that aren’t being met. Whatever the reason, notice that the closing is something you are doing. It’s not happening to you; you are actively pulling back, resisting, tightening. The key is to stop doing that. Let go of the fears and unmet preferences that make you contract. If you do that, your heart will open on its own.



As you work through this, you’ll notice something profound. When you stop closing, you’ll start experiencing life more fully. You’ll feel other people’s emotions more deeply, and sometimes you’ll feel pain more intensely. That’s not a problem—that’s what it means to be open. When someone shares their struggles with you and your heart aches, don’t resist. That’s your heart awakening, coming alive. The reason you haven’t felt that before is because you were too busy protecting yourself.

If you truly want to live with an open heart, make it your practice to let go of yourself. Stop filtering life through “What do I need? What do I want?” Instead, shift your attention outward. Be more interested in others than yourself. Be present for them, without needing anything in return. It’s really not that hard to have an open heart—just stop closing it.

19-2.q: How should one handle fluctuations in the experience of love and joy?
19-2.a:
The first thing you need to understand is that it’s not your job to control the experiences of love and joy. Your heart knows exactly what it’s doing. Just like your body has an immune system that takes care of itself, your heart has its own process of opening, expanding, and cleansing. When love pours through you, it’s because something inside has opened. When it seems to fade or contract, it’s because something deeper is being worked through. It’s not a problem—it’s part of the process.

There will be times when love expands so much that you don’t know how to handle it. It can feel overwhelming, even scary, because it’s pushing you beyond the limits of what you are comfortable feeling. Then there will be times when it feels like love is gone. But just like waves in the ocean, love isn’t disappearing—it’s just cycling through its natural rhythm. When it pulls back, trust that it’s doing what it needs to do. Maybe it’s bringing up something that needs to be released. Maybe it’s preparing to open even further. Either way, it’s none of your business. Your only job is to let go and allow it to do its work.

You have to stop trying to manage love. The mind wants to ask, How do I keep it? How do I make it stay? But the heart isn’t something you hold on to—it’s something you surrender into. The more you try to control it, the further away it gets. So when love comes, let it come fully. When it seems to fade, give it the space it needs. It’s still there, just working at a deeper level.

The truth is, love wants to take you further than you can imagine. For that to happen, you have to be willing to let it have you completely. That means letting go of yourself—your resistance and fears, even your ideas of what love is supposed to feel like. Just let go completely and thank love for the journey.

19-3.q: It is often taught that the heart center is divided into two halves, lower and higher. Does that still apply when the heart is open?
19-3.a:
If your heart is open, the idea of it being divided into halves is not something that applies in the way you might think. The division isn’t a structural one— it’s about how much of your heart you’re actually willing to open. There’s a lower half to the heart center, where you experience love in a personal way, and then there’s the higher half, where love is no longer personal—it just is. If you stay in the lower part, your love is conditional. It depends on people behaving a certain way, looking a certain way, doing what you want them to do. That’s personal love, and it comes with all kinds of struggles and expectations. It’s not the highest love.

If you let go of yourself enough, you don’t place conditions on love anymore. Instead of holding on to personal attachments, you move into a space where love is always there, flowing freely. This isn’t something you manufacture—it’s something that exists beyond the personal self. The love that comes from above is always available, and when you open fully, you are no longer withholding it or filtering it through your personal wants and fears. It becomes unconditional.

As long as you continue to open, the division dissolves. You aren’t stuck in a lower or higher half—you’re simply open. The more you let go, the more open your heart becomes, and the more naturally love flows. If you close, even just a little, you create resistance. That’s when conditions creep back in.

Ultimately, the heart isn’t meant to be divided. The only question is whether you are allowing it to be fully open. And the answer to that isn’t found in trying to make love fit into your personal framework; it’s found in letting go of yourself completely, so that love can exist as it truly is.

19-4.q: If I already feel unconditional love within myself, what would a love relationship with someone else look like?
19-4.a:
If you are already feeling unconditional love within yourself, then loving another person is simply an expression of that love. You are not looking to get love from them, nor are you relying on them to behave a certain way in order for you to feel whole. You are already whole. The love you feel is not dependent on another person; it is something you honor within yourself and then share. That is the essence of real love. It is not about fulfilling needs, expectations, or conditions. It is about allowing the love that already exists within you to flow freely, without resistance, no matter what happens.

When you bring another person into the equation, old patterns, expectations, fears, and desires will naturally arise within you. Your partner’s behavior will not always align perfectly with what you might want, and this will stir up inner reactions. Your work is to recognize these reactions as blockages that prevent love from flowing unconditionally. Your challenge is to not let them close you. No one outside of you can close your heart—only you can do that. If you are truly committed to unconditional love, you must make the decision that no matter what happens, you will not close.

Not closing is what love is really about. It is not about whether the other person reciprocates in the way you think they should. Love is simply the act of keeping your heart open, regardless of circumstances. If someone brings up things in you that feel difficult, that’s okay. In fact, that’s the gift of relationships—they show you the places inside where you’re still holding on, where you’re not free. Rather than seeing a relationship as something you need to control, see it as an opportunity to go deeper into yourself by letting go of anything that would cause you to close.
